The positive characteristics of hadron production from a high-energy heavy-ion synchrotron, combined with the high momentum capacity of a muon collider, suggest that a muon-ion synchrotron could achieve unprecedented TeV-scale energies for hadrons and muons. This concept can be realized using a next-generation HEP collider design, and I argue that a muon-ion synchrotron has the potential to break through technical limitations in other types of colliders. Specifically, it could produce the highest energies for protons, heavy ions, and muons, and also enable precise low-intensity beams for neutrino and muon-based experiments. Furthermore, a muon-ion synchrotron can serve as a versatile machine that supports multiple purposes, including HEP, materials science, and industrial applications, and its large size and robust design make it an ideal facility for global collaboration and collaboration with other industries. Some potential applications and research areas for a TeV-scale muon-ion synchrotron include studying non-linear QCD, investigating new physics beyond the Standard Model, searching for dark matter and dark energy, investigating the muon anomalous magnetic moment, and exploring new facilities for particle physics, such as a next-generation $B$-factory or a CP-violation factory. This research paper proposes a novel approach to developing secure and robust controllers for complex nonlinear control systems. Our innovative method builds upon the concepts of Control Barrier Functions, which were initially introduced to devise feasible and efficient controllers. However, potential issues with the original approach led to the creation of the Re-Reachable Control Barrier Functions, which enhances its performance. To overcome the limitation of requiring full control authority across the entire feasible region, we introduced the concept of Controlled Preconditions at the boundary, which enables the development of a more efficient and secure controller. Our proposed framework includes two main strategies: one for definite security and one for contingent security, depending on whether the initial state lies within the feasible region or not. Theoretical proof of our method's validity and three practical applications serve as illustration of its usefulness. Furthermore, an open-source tool called "RRCBF" is also introduced to facilitate the design of controllable regions and the computation of preconditions through numerical optimization. This allows for the creation of displays illustrating the region of controllability and preconditions through 3D plotting. Additionally, the paper explores the relationship between our approach and continuous control barrier functions, confirming which conditions are met for a globally defined function along with discussing the scope and limitations of our method. Our proposed framework offers an engaging case study involving an autonomous aerial vehicle in the form of a tutorial on how to utilize the "RRCBF" open-source tool. This includes step-by-step instructions and the detailed code required to design the controller, the controlled preconditions and the 3D preconditions display, as well as the configuration of the "PyCCBF" interface. This will allow other researchers to reproduce the results and explore the vast possibilities offered by the "RRCBF" and "PyCCBF" suites of tools. In this work, we establish a novel representation for the area measurements in CF-approximation spaces, a recent and highly versatile framework. We demonstrate that any CF-approximation space can serve as a reliable measure for determining unique values, and that this fundamental aspect underlies the efficacy of CF-approximation spaces. Building on this foundation, we explore the broader implications and identify the inherent connections between CF-approximation spaces and established concepts like Hausdorff measures. Additionally, we introduce a new criterion for predicting whether a function is measurable within a CF-approximation space, and we show that the common Carathéodory measure can be viewed as a specific instance of a CF-approximation space. Finally, we highlight the potential for further exploration into CF-approximation spaces, particularly in relation to geometric measure theory. 

In the companion article [1], we examine the relationship between CF-approximation spaces and the theory of functions, while in the companion article [2] we explore the connection between CF-approximation spaces and the theory of geometric measure, among other topics.

The accuracy of structural equation modeling (SEM) results relies heavily on the quality of model fit statistics, which are commonly derived from nonlinear functions of maximum likelihood estimates.
This paper proposes an innovative technique called paired-permutation estimation (PPE) to calculate the standard error of the chi-square test statistic and other fit measures, such as the robust fit index and the Bayesian information criterion, without relying on asymptotic theory.
The PPE framework involves exchanging the observations of adjacent cases within a data set and recalculating the SEM model for each pair, resulting in an initial set of model fit statistics.
A second round of calculations is then conducted on a revised data set constructed from the means of those pairs, producing a second set of model fit statistics, which serve as the reference against which the consistency and accuracy of the PPE estimates are evaluated.
The results of a simulation study suggest that the standard errors generated by PPE are reliable and accurately represented, and the method compares favorably to existing alternatives in terms of computational efficiency.
The code for implementing PPE in R has been made available with the proposed method and can be integrated into the SEM AMOS interface via the R AMOS (RAM) package. Furthermore, a new version of the semj package, which includes the PPE function, has been developed and is now available on CRAN. The PPE technique is a generalizable framework that can be applied to a wide range of statistical tests with complex distributions and is particularly suited for use with large data sets. The proposed method offers several advantages over the conventional delta method and bootstrapping techniques, including better performance and a more intuitive understanding of results, as subject matter experts are already familiar with the standard error concept. The results of the simulation study, along with an examination of the performance of SEM models, suggest that the PPE method is an enhanced alternative to traditional methods and is currently the most efficient technique available. By focusing on the relationships among objects rather than their absolute positions, we represent such systems using "fabric spaces" – a theoretical framework that encompasses various guises like configuration spaces, arrangement spaces, and Voronoi diagrams. Embracing a discrete, combinatorial approach, we leverage the concept of "persistent simplicial structures" to analyze the evolving topology of these systems over time. A specific discrete framework, "triangulation paths," provides a comprehensive understanding of the topological transformations occurring within fabric spaces. Moreover, this framework enables the identification of meaningful patterns in the data obtained from the topological observations, which we call "topological features." A prominent example of such features is the emergence of Betti numbers, whose roles in physics and biology are well-documented. Another significant feature is the collection of "wiring diagrams," which describe the internal structure of Voronoi complexes and reveal information about the underlying system's dynamics. Building upon these concepts are higher-level features like "topological phase transitions" and "geometric structures," which can be seen as the union of discrete and continuous aspects. Ultimately, this study paves the way for a broader exploration of the principles underlying topological models, realizing that such models are an expression of the interplay between a system's geometry and its topological structure, which gives rise to the combinatorial approach adopted here. This perspective is further illustrated through the examination of a non-conservative, first-order phase transition process, for which the provided framework reveals novel evidence of a underlying force that directs the system's behavior, leading to the conclusion that this type of transition may, in fact, be an exception rather than the rule. This exception is characterized by a specific "wiring diagram" known as the N-diagram, whose structure may represent a fundamental property of time-fluctuation geometries. Spinning superfluids exhibit unique behavior as they transition from a solid lattice of vortices to a swirling liquid.  The heat added to this process ultimately powers the spin-up.  A team led by Prof. Kevork Abraamian from the University of Copenhagen's QMC group used a measurement technique called Nernst effect to gain insight into this transition.  By measuring the resistance of a thin gold track as a temperature and spin-up rate varied, the researchers were able to create detailed pictures of the vortex state as the spin-up rate changed - a task previously made difficult by the lack of a clear definition of the vortex state as vortices blend together to form a continuous'sea'.  The findings show that the viscosity of the vortex liquid is actually lower than expected and the researchers were also able to create a theoretical model to explain the observed patterns.  The model highlights the role that the entropy of the fluid plays in its behavior, a factor that is often overlooked in similar studies.  The work has been published in the prestigious scientific journal 'Physical Review Letters' and is expected to contribute significantly to the advancement of scientific knowledge in the field of superfluids. The most effective solution to modeling complex uncertainties in real-time dynamic systems involves leveraging historical performance data and adaptable controllers. However, existing model-based approaches can struggle with rapid changes, especially in systems subject to external influences that can impact individual component behavior. In such cases, prioritizing the optimization of individual components can lead to inefficient solutions that fail to consider the broader system impacts. In our research, we focus on energy management systems that can complicate the modeling process due to the inherent differences between continuous and on-off control of various assets. In collaboration with Google's machine learning experts, we've developed a novel predictive control framework that utilizes gradient boosting decision trees to analyze refined performance metrics associated with each asset group. By directly optimizing these metrics, which reflect the overall system performance, our approach overcomes the limitations of individual component optimization. Furthermore, our solution avoids the need to estimate external influences and adaptively addresses potential discrepancies between historical and real-time data patterns. In our experiments using real-world data from a large commercial building, our approach has demonstrated superior performance compared to traditional model predictive control methods. In particular, we've observed a significant improvement in overall system performance, along with reduced energy consumption and lower carbon emissions. In some scenarios, our solution even managed to minimize the variability of asset group outputs in real-time, resulting in better matching of historical and actual performance patterns. In our energy management application, our approach has successfully handled up to 20 distinct asset groups with unique performance metrics in real-time, providing a promising solution for addressing similar data-driven control challenges in other domains. In our research, we've also explored the use of alternative machine learning algorithms within our framework and have gathered preliminary results indicating that our approach can be adapted to accommodate other gradient boosting methods. In our energy management setting, we found that our solution could be readily applied to Google's AI-accelerated platform, running on remote servers and providing real-time control instructions to the building's management system via a high-bandwidth network connection. In our experiments, we've successfully deployed our solution on a Google Tensor Processing Unit (TPU) cloud-based sandbox, running at a significantly lower cost compared to traditional model predictive control methods. We developed a theoretical model that describes the drag force the cylinder experiences due to its shape within the granular medium, whose parameters include the ratio of the cylinder's diameter to the distance between grains and the rate at which the fluid saturates the space around the cylinder. This model is compared to multiple experiments using various sizes of cylinders, different types of grains, and various fluid saturations. This anisotropy of drag force may be of use in further research on the transport of objects moving through complex fluids within granular media and potentially in a wide range of natural and industrial processes. Astronomers have a comprehensive understanding of how star formation is linked to gas motions in galaxies, but the impact of gas outflows on star formation remains less clear. Using the KMOS line package on VLT/KMOS, a study of a starburst galaxy (NGC 4495) found initial results indicative of an outflow's effect on star formation. Upon reanalyzing existing data with an optimal analysis method (DVelt), researchers discovered enhanced signals and a more pronounced effect of the outflow on star formation, supporting the idea that outflows suppress star formation in a galaxy's center. This effect was seen to extend to the outer regions of the galaxy. Additionally, a connection between the outflow's kinetic energy and a suppression of star formation was demonstrated, providing insight into the physical relationship between outflows and star formation. A link between the outflow's direction and a star formation suppression effect was also identified, suggesting a critical role for the galaxy's geometry in determining the outflows' impact on star formation. A comparison with burst galaxy models (BUK) revealed that DVelt's analysis method is sensitive to a galaxy's mass, while an analysis of a sample of 15 galaxies revealed a correlation between a galaxy's mass and the outflows' effect on star formation, with more massive galaxies exhibiting a greater outflow-star formation link. This discovery was made possible by the high spatial resolution and multi-line observations provided by KMOS. A further investigation into the outflows' effect on star formation, guided by a simple model, showed that a collapse of the galaxy's disk may generate an outflow that then suppresses star formation, a process that can create a link between the outflows and star formation in galaxies. This relationship was found to be a transient one, with a duration set by the time it takes a gas disk to collapse. A study of a sample of 15 galaxies using a simple model also revealed an outflows-star formation link in galaxies with a disk that is in the process of collapsing, as well as in a galaxy that is experiencing a minor starburst, with the outflows-star formation link being a more persistent feature in the latter. A study of a burst galaxy (Mrk 1034) observed in both its active and dormant states provided further evidence for an outflows-star formation link, with a comparison of the two states using a simple model indicating that the outflows' effect on star formation is a transient one, with a duration set by the time it takes a gas disk to collapse. Our research examined the triangular flow coefficient $v_3$ within a multiphase transport model, particularly for 200 GeV Au+Au and Cu+Cu collisions. Initially, our simulation results for $v_3$ exhibited negative values at high transverse momenta, yet after incorporating an initial anisotropic momentum distribution, these negative values disappeared. However, we discovered that final anisotropic flows could still be reproduced without any external influence, yet only if initial conditions were taken into account. Notably, initial conditions played a significant role in determining final anisotropic flows. Additionally, our analysis demonstrated that initial anisotropic fluctuations may not be the primary driver of anisotropic flow emissions from the medium itself. Furthermore, without considering the effects of radial flow, our research found that elliptical flow could be made independent of $v_3$, yet only if initial anisotropic fluctuations are taken into account. Conversely, we found that when radial flow is accounted for, $v_3$ actually decreases with rising impact parameter in Au+Au collisions, a trend that is consistent with experimental data. By contrast, in Cu+Cu collisions, $v_3$ remains unaffected by changes in impact parameter. Our research also revealed that the amplitude of initial anisotropic fluctuations over broad momentum ranges may be as low as 0.006, which could be considered a relatively modest value. Furthermore, our analysis indicated that flucutations in the equation of state may lead to increased anisotropic flow. Moreover, our research demonstrated that anisotropic flow in 200 GeV Au+Au collisions may be understood through the lens of anisotropic initial conditions, whereas additional mechanisms may be necessary to explain anisotropic flow in lower energy collisions. Lastly, our study found that anisotropic flow is not solely driven by light quark propagation, as the dependence of anisotropic flow on quark flavor appears to be flavor-independent. Instead, our analysis indicates that anisotropic flow may be influenced more significantly by light and heavy diquark fluctuations. Which in turn may imply that diquarks propagate differently than quarks within the QCD medium. Our research provides a starting point for a more in-depth examination of the interplay between fundamental quark properties and anisotropic flow. Ultimately, our study suggests that anisotropic flow may serve as a crucial tool in unraveling the intricate nature of the QCD medium. Over the years, the availability of Linked Data has surged exponentially with more than 10,000 online datasets now available and formatted according to Linked Data standards, enabling seamless machine readability and interconnectivity.  While such datasets provide numerous opportunities, numerous applications remain hindered due to the lack of reliable and efficient quality assessment tools, primarily due to the complex and distributed nature of RDF datasets, making existing QA techniques less applicable.  Existing approaches, tailored for traditional data formats, fail to account for the distinct characteristics of Linked Data, such as URI references, whereas existing structureless and user-based evaluation methods are not scalable or efficient.  To address these limitations, we introduce an innovative, scalable quality assessment framework, tailored for Linked Data, featuring a novel metric that evaluates data quality based on numerous criteria, including uniqueness, data completeness, functional data integrity, functional data utility, and functional data coherence.  This framework is particularly useful for large-scale Linked Data, such as Lehigh University Answer Sets (LUAS), which comprises over 17 million triples.  Our experimental evaluations, conducted on both small-scale and large-scale Linked Data, demonstrate that our proposed approach outperforms existing methods, yielding superior results in terms of precision, while our designed prototype ensures ease-of-use and minimal required user expertise.  Our innovative quality assessment framework, complemented by an insightful discussion on existing approaches, our methodology, and our experimental setup, along with our conducted evaluations, provides a comprehensive foundation for developing effective and scalable data quality assessment methods, tailored for the ever-expanding Linked Data landscape.  As part of this research, we also introduce two novel data quality evaluation methods, along with a novel structure for summarizing evaluation outcomes, which can be applied to both structured and semantic data.  Our work on structuring and publishing the results of data quality evaluations, along with our discussion on the challenges associated with conducting such evaluations, can serve as a model for other researchers and practitioners in the field of Linked Data.  Furthermore, our experience with conducting data quality evaluations, combined with our discussion on the importance of replication, has guided us to make available for replication all the data and configuration used in this study.  Additionally, our work has inspired us to explore potential applications of data quality evaluations in the context of Semantic Web Services, Quality of Service, and Web Service Composition.  As part of this research, we have also investigated the potential integration of our proposed approach with existing techniques for detecting and repairing data errors, as well as the potential extension of our quality evaluation framework to accommodate other criteria

Detecting three-dimensional objects at great distances is a crucial and demanding task in 3D object detection. Distant objects pose difficulty due to limited points belonging to them, often causing existing methods to focus on nearby objects rather than distant ones during training. This means that even if distant objects are labeled, the model may not learn from them, leading to a lack of capability to detect distant objects in practice. This paper proposes Far3Det, a new distant 3D object detection task evaluation metric and benchmark, along with corresponding protocols, to guide the development of specialized models that excel in detecting distant objects. Distant object detection requires modeling the object's distance, which is intricately linked to scaling and aspect ratio. To achieve this, we introduce a distance-aware box and incorporate it into a RetinaNet-based detector to enhance detection performance. Experimental results on Far3Det demonstrate the efficacy of our approach in surpassing state-of-the-art benchmarks. Furthermore, we find that transferring knowledge from Far3Det to the near-3D detection task yields beneficial effects, indicating that distinct models may be necessary for optimizing detection performance in the near and distant object scales. This registration method has been successfully integrated with a surface extraction tool and two landmarking techniques for brain imaging, yielding promising results compared to established non-rigid registration methods. This registration method holds promise for accurate measurements of soft tissue deformation, particularly suitable for applications involving minimal deformation and easily identifiable landmarks. Determining scene flow involves calculating the three-dimensional motion trajectories for specific points within an animated three-dimensional environment. This computation is challenging due to real-world data constraints and the complexity of the task. Real-world datasets, such as KITTI, contain noisy label information, with the flow velocities often exceeding the maximum possible velocity for a vehicle. Existing evaluation metrics for scene flow estimation algorithms are based on the ground truth provided by optical flow algorithms and do not account for real-world noise, creating a need for a more realistic evaluation approach. The standard mean squared error metric has significant issues including its sensitivity to the selection of nearest neighbor counterparts, especially in dense areas where the choice of neighbor can result in inaccurate error calculations. A new evaluation approach and a more robust metric learning method are introduced in this research to address these challenges. The evaluation approach is called the self-guided metric flow (SGMF) evaluation, which uses a model that is trained to calculate the optimal nearest neighbor distance for each 3D point autonomously. This results in lower errors compared to traditional methods and showcases the practical applications of metric learning in real-world 3D vision tasks. The introduced SGMF evaluation framework and its associated metric learning model, the self-guided metric flow (SGMF) model, outperform existing state-of-the-art scene flow estimation algorithms while achieving this by utilizing much simpler models that require significantly less training and computation. The code for the proposed method has been made available online at https://github.com/kaustuvghose/selfguided-metric-learning. The results for this research are presented at the IEEE Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (CVPR) in 2023. The inspiration for this research originated from the PASCAL Visual Object Classes (VOC) challenge's spray paint scenario, which depicts animated 3D point environments, however the primary focus shifted to analyzing real-world datasets such as KITTI. For a given irreducible polynomial $f$, we define the block arrangement as a collection of hypersurfaces corresponding to the coefficients of $f$, and investigate its properties. Notably, we establish connections between the prime values of $|f(\alpha_1, \alpha_2, \ldots, \alpha_k)|$ and the configuration of hyperplanes in the block arrangement, for specific types of polynomials such as Recaman primes and the prime values of the Frobenius polynomial. Additionally, we explore applications of these results to quantify the number of prime values of polynomials, including those induced by geometric linear constructions and Construction A, extending previous works by Browwer, Schur, and Bergman in the field of geometry. Furthermore, our results demonstrate the prime value distribution of some polynomials exceeds the expectations set by the Bateman-Horn conjecture, with a focus on the analysis of the prime values of polynomials generated by Construction A and geometric linear constructions, revealing an explicit prime value count in some cases and an implicit connection to the prime value distribution in others. Finally, we observe that certain block arrangements yield a finite nonabelian simple group, providing an additional theoretical framework and potentially useful tools in the study of the prime values of polynomials. The developed methods can be applied to a broader class of polynomials, revealing new examples of the prime values of polynomials that arise from the intersection of hyperplanes, construction of symmetric polynomials, and the application of the fundamental theorem of finite fields. The research also sheds light on the relationship between the prime values of polynomials and the configuration of hyperplanes, paving the way for further exploration of the connections between number theory and geometry. This paper introduces a new approach called Timeloops for automating system call policy learning across multiple programs, particularly those containerized microservices. Unlike traditional static analysis methods, Timeloops leverages a novel form of automated testing to rapidly identify policy violations and optimize performance. A key innovation within Timeloops is a novel "what happened when" debugging technique called Whipt, which is both efficient and precise. To demonstrate the effectiveness of Timeloops, we apply it to a sample e-commerce microservice, Whipt in combination with a basic implementation being shown to achieve a 2.5x performance improvement over a baseline approach. Furthermore, our research showcases the versatility of Timeloops, Whipt's versatility also leading to a 5x improvement in learning time when compared to other learning-based methods. The source code for both Timeloops and Whipt has been made publicly available. Additionally, we introduce a new challenge problem for the Policy Learning Challenge (PLC) at ICSME 2021, which serves as a benchmark for Timeloops' Whipt. Deep learning-based 3D LiDAR location recognition systems can be particularly useful in highly dynamic environments for vehicles. Current techniques typically employ a end-to-end design, where a single network predicts both the location and orientation, or a two-stage approach where a separate network detects features from a set of candidate locations. Streaming high-quality video is increasingly dependent on the efficient processing of video bits streams. A key challenge arises when these streams require transcoding, as a single misconfigured or underpowered cloud server can compromise the viewing experience for many users. In response, using multiple cloud servers from different pools can be beneficial, but this raises questions about how to allocate resources effectively and what impact the choice of cloud providers has on the overall system. Additionally, we explore related questions regarding the p-adic volume of K and its subfield. This research is motivated by recent work connecting Leopoldt-type theorems and the p-adic volume of number fields. We establish the result for some widely used Galois groups, including GLn(Ql), Syd(n, Ql), and GLn(FQl) for local fields F = Qp or F = Q_s, and we provide an update on ongoing research with R. This study provides a critical evaluation of the contextualized language models and methods used for analyzing diachronic semantic data. We examined the methods used for word sense stabilization and ranking words by their degree of semantic change. Through extensive experimentation, our findings reveal that current methods face numerous challenges, including the inherent fluctuations in word sense frequencies and the difficulties in word sense disambiguation. We discovered that imposing word sense constraints through techniques like Bayesian learning and multiple clustering methods can lead to improvements in measuring semantic change. However, these constraints cannot fully mitigate the issues with diachronic data, which are characterized by a high degree of noise and a limited time span for the study period. We also found that the contextualized language models are capable of capturing the inherent fluctuations in word sense frequencies and the challenges associated with diachronic data, which are reflected in the inherent fluctuations in word sense distributions. Ultimately, our research highlights the limitations of diachronic data and the difficulties in word sense disambiguation, which pose significant obstacles for any analysis of the data. As such, we do not prescribe a specific approach but instead offer our methodological framework and our observations on the inherent properties of diachronic data, which are equally applicable to the analysis of semantic change in word embeddings. Additionally, we include a comprehensive word set that can be used for comparing and evaluating any methodology used for analyzing diachronic semantic change. Using statistical models of quasars' luminosity and black hole mass, we calculate the average spin rate of quasars, finding it consistent with a model relying on a specific ultralight boson mass range. This range, determined by the spin rate and the probability of boson emission, dictates the mass of the ultralight boson, which may explain the variety of quasars' spin rates. Additionally, we identify two categories of quasars based on their spin rates: those with elevated spin rates, fitting an ultra-light standard model; and those with lower spin rates, fitting a model where the standard ultralight boson is replaced with a more massive boson, assuming a specific minimum mass threshold for stable ultralight bosons as required by supersradiance. Notably, the most substantial objects with the lowest spin rates, classified as "quasar binaries," have the most accurate measurements of the standard ultralight boson mass range. These findings contribute to the investigation of the ultralight standard model, offering a hypothesis to explain the absence of high-energy spectral lines from quasars and binary systems containing accreting black holes. Normally, these singularities appear at high energies and their extraordinary version is thought to occur in systems with substantial gaps in the energy spectrum. In contrast, a broader range of research suggests that the perception of agency and animacy is interconnected and influenced by multiple factors, including action-related information and the presentation of static postures. However, current galaxy formation models are hindered by a lack of precision in the mass-scale of these star clusters due to limited observational data. Developing a scalable relationship between the radii of these star clusters and their mass is one possible solution, but existing scaling laws are limited by their reliance on ground-based measurements, which are prone to biases. This study presents an extensive and precise mapping of the radius-mass relation of star clusters within five galaxies (NGC 4605, NGC 4697, NGC 4762, NGC 4871, and NGC 5107) using the high-resolution, space-based data from the Hubble Space Telescope. This approach bypasses the system's bias from $SU(3)_f$ symmetry breaking, allowing for more precise estimates. As an application, we calculate the decay width of $\eta_c$ into two photons using this method, yielding $\Gamma_{\eta_c \rightarrow \gamma\gamma} = 0.648^{+0.078}_{0.076}$ keV, which compares to the current lattice QCD result of $0.695^{+0.0075}_{0.0072}$ keV. Additionally, we explore the possibility of extracting the electromagnetic form factor of mesons from this technique. As an aside, we also provide estimates for the decay widths of $\eta_b$ into two photons and a bottomonium mixing phenomenon. Furthermore, corrections for the volume effects in our direct method are discussed, with the findings that the volume effects are negligible for the $\eta_c$ and $\eta_b$ cases at the relevant lattice spacings. Lastly, we detail an alternative approach for computing the decay width, which involves direct lattice unitary transformations, and find this method to be less efficient but still feasible. Nonetheless, our primary focus remains on the novel technique introduced at the outset. Moreover, we observe that both methods converge with increasing exponent sizes, yielding consistent outcomes with the current lattice QCD results for the decay widths of $\eta_c$ and $\eta_b$ into two photons. Our novel technique offers an alternative solution to the issue of volume effects in finite-volume lattice QCD studies, without which the proposed method would result in significant underestimation of the decay width. This finding, in turn, raises the question of how widely this issue might be relevant across other lattice QCD applications. Lastly, we note that both proposed methods rely on the use of multiple exponential fits, which are known to be susceptible to system uncertainties and ambiguities in extrapolating lattice data to the continuum limit. Recent breakthroughs in numerical methods, such as the Hubbard-Stratonovich transformation and the bosonization technique, have made it possible to solve for the ground states in correlated quantum systems. These solutions can then be used to train artificial neural networks, allowing them to accurately model complex data and solve unstructured problems. However, the Hubward Sign problem poses a significant challenge to these approaches, causing the networks to become unstable and limiting them to only modeling states with positive signs. In the case of fermionic systems, such as half-filling one-dimensional Hubbard models, this sign problem cannot be overcome with conventional transformations and typically results in the networks experiencing a significant increase in variance or having to be trained from scratch for each separate sector. This not only hinders the ability to generalizes across different system sizes but also limits the ability to generalize across different fillings. In this letter, we introduce a novel transformation that eliminates the sign problem altogether, allowing the networks to be trained in a unified manner across different fillings. As a result, the networks exhibit improved performance on the data obtained from multiple sectors, significantly reducing the number of training examples needed and allowing them to generalize across different system sizes and fillings. In addition, we find that this new transformation also mitigates the excessive increase in variance, making it possible to model systems with large system sizes and multiple sector bases. In 1982, Gruenberg established a significant link between the boolean structures of a set's involution and its polynomial size, specifically in the context of boolean functions over a single variable. This thesis chapter delves into the world of boolean structures of involutions, a theory initially described by T.Q. Bui and Le Ngoc Thanh in 2013. A key aspect of this theory involves the boolean structures of partial functions with involutions, which we examine and characterize through the lens of Gruenberg's original work. This characterization serves as a fundamental proof of the limitations of certain circuits comprising involutions, which we demonstrate can be realized with significantly more gates than their non-involutive counterparts. Finally, we explore an expansion of this theory to the boolean structures of multi-variable functions with involutions, a previously unexamined area. By applying our previous results and incorporating an intriguing connection to the field of algebra, specifically semigroups, we arrive at an expanded version of the boolean structures of involutions, a theoretical framework that we then apply to derive new circuit size lower bound proofs. These new proofs not only provide a more general framework for previous results but also yield novel lower bound insights, which we anticipate will be of further interest to researchers in the field. This thesis chapter is a comprehensive exploration of the boolean structures of involutions, a rich and complex area that we believe warrants continued exploration and research. As we bring this chapter to a close, we look forward to the potential future contributions that future studies in this area will undoubtedly bring. We created an advanced statistical model to map the Milky Way's disk population and identify moving patterns of stars. This model utilized vast amounts of data from the APOGEE-2 survey and included external factors such as the position of the sun and the orientation of the galaxy's disk. By applying a two-measurement approach and accounting for random sampling errors, our findings revealed six distinct groups of stars within the galaxy's disk region, each consisting of specific elements such as carbon-rich and oxygen-rich main sequence stars, as well as blue horizontal red giants. Furthermore, our research discovered additional patterns of stars in the galaxy, including twenty-three separate clusters, often referred to as "moving groups" or "chemically distinct populations." These findings were validated through multiple independent analyses and were based on a wide range of measurements including positions, movements, and chemical compositions. Additionally, our study demonstrated that a vast majority of the stars in the galaxy's disk region are part of these moving patterns, accounting for approximately seventy-five percent of the data, while a smaller group of fourteen distinct clusters consisted of only about one and a half percent of the data. These clusters generally consisted of rare or unique stars such as low-mass stars, white dwarfs, and pulsating giant stars. On the other hand, our study also identified smaller patterns of stars that could not be confirmed through multiple independent analyses, often due to certain limitations or biases in the data, such as the angle from which the galaxy is viewed, which affected the visibility of certain stars in the outer regions. Furthermore, our research indicated that certain features of the galaxy, such as the curve of the sun's path and the shape of the galaxy's center, did not show any clear patterns of moving stars. Additionally, our study demonstrated that the galaxy's disk population consists of a wide range of different ages, extending as far as twelve billion years into the past, while our research on the chemical composition of the galaxy's moving patterns revealed a complex relationship between the formation of stars and the distribution of elements, often referred to as abundance patterns, which are created by the explosion of ancient super-novae and the formation of new stars. The COVID-19 pandemic spread rapidly around the world, causing widespread disruption and affecting every aspect of life.  As the virus continued to mutate and adapt, rumors and misinformation posed a significant threat, potentially diverting crucial attention and resources from lifesaving measures.  To examine this issue further, our research analyzed online rumors and their transmission in China during the initial outbreak phase.  We introduced the concept of a "super-spreader" user - a particular individual whose actions significantly contribute substantially to the rapid dissemination of a rumor.  Through the application of time-series analysis and modeling, we found that the rate at which rumors are shared follows a distinct pattern over time, with certain keywords contributing substantially to the acceleration or slowing down of this process.  By identifying and removing these "super-spreader" users and adjusting for temporal effects as well as the impact of keywords, we were able to evaluate the genuine influence of various transmission pathway lengths.  Our results show that a significant proportion of rumors are transmitted directly between users, with smaller but still notable percentages of rumors being shared through longer pathways.  Furthermore, our research highlights the critical difference between initially believed rumors and those later disproven, with the former more likely to be shared by users with higher credibility and the latter more likely to be disseminated through longer pathways.  Additionally, our analysis reveals that the credibility of the user who initially posts a rumor has a more significant impact on its transmission than the credibility of the user who ultimately confirms the rumor.  With the aim of developing more effective counter-measures against the spread of online rumors, our research provides a theoretical basis for the creation of a suite of metrics and tools to assess the transmission and impact of these rumors.  We also explore the connection between the dissemination of online rumors and the emergence of COVID-19-related misinformation on Wikipedia, an event-driven cumulative stimulus response model.  Lastly, we discuss the broader implications and potential applications of our research in addressing the difficult issue of online rumor dissemination.  As the pace of information sharing accelerates in the digital world, the transmission of false information has the potential to cause significant harm, making the development of the Dissemination Computer System a critical priority.  This system can provide insights into the spread of online rumors, the emergence of events-driven phenomena, and the impact of user behavior on the transmission of false information.  Furthermore, this research can be adapted to combat the dissemination of malicious software, the spread of disease, and other cumulative stimulus response phenomena observed in complex networks. This research paper proposes a stream processing engine called LifeStream, which is designed to efficiently manage periodic data flows. Traditional stream processing systems are typically used for event-driven applications, but they often employ a cumbersome and costly approach to manage periodic data. In contrast, LifeStream leverages a novel, low-cost scheduling mechanism called the Time-Space-Order scheduling approach, combining data preloading and a specific sorting method. By minimizing the need for restarts and re-sorting, LifeStream significantly improves the performance of periodic data processing. The proposed system also includes several key features such as dynamic scaling, user-defined aggregation functions, and an easy-to-use SQL interface. The advantages of LifeStream are exemplified through a case study of a real-world application, demonstrating a 5x performance boost and 1.5x reduction in costs when using LifeStream. The system's efficiency results in lowered infrastructure expenses, achieving a 5% overall cost savings. The source code of LifeStream has been made available on GitHub, enabling the integration of Time-Space-Order scheduling into other Apache Flink clusters. A widely adopted modification in deep learning research involves adjusting the loss function to match the decision-making process of the model's final activation function, which we explored in this study. We examined various loss function modifications, analyzed their mathematical underpinnings, and discussed practical considerations for using them. A comprehensive evaluation was conducted across multiple datasets, activation functions, and network architectures to determine the effects on performance. Our results showed that making these adjustments can lead to improved classification accuracy, but the benefits may not always justify the increased computational costs due to more complex optimization processes. Ultimately, our research provides insights for practitioners to make informed decisions about using unmodified or adjusted loss functions in deep learning for classification tasks. We also open-source our evaluation framework for the benefit of the broader research community.

A stabilizable boundary feedback controller is designed for the Navier-Stokes equations using a flat control surface in a two-dimensional flow domain. By analyzing the spectrum of the Navier-Stokes operator with the boundary feedback term, we demonstrate the possibility of achieving exponential stability for the system. A key aspect of our approach involves transforming the original boundary feedback control problem into an equivalent interior control problem, which is then addressed through the use of a boundary observation operator in a Hilbert space setting. This strategy of reformulating the boundary control problem as an interior control problem can be applied more broadly, as shown by a counterexample highlighting the limitation of previous methods. One of the key challenges in teaching robots via positive reinforcement learning is ensuring they understand what behaviors are desired. To overcome this limitation, robots can be trained using a different approach with corrective guidance, which involves learning from corrections or feedback about their actions. However, the current state-of-the-art in machine learning does not effectively generalize learning algorithms for natural inputs to robots that provide precise, high-dimensional feedback. In this paper, we introduce a theoretical framework that identifies key differences between natural and digital guidance and demonstrates how existing learning algorithms can be adapted to succeed with corrective guidance. We also address several critical issues in learning from digital feedback, including the need for robust algorithms that aren't sensitive to the high-dimensional feedback provided by the environment and the need for the agent to learn from this feedback while exploring its physical world. We validated our approach with an experiment involving a robotic grasping task and found that existing learning algorithms can be adapted to successfully learn from corrective guidance on a physical robot using only a digital model of the task. Our results show that our approach leads to significant improvements in performance when compared to learning from random corrections. We were also able to achieve near-expert performance when compared to a robot that is trained using both positive and corrective feedback. In addition, we found that our approach allows the agent to learn from a smaller number of corrections and that our algorithms are more sample-efficient than the state-of-the-art method for learning from random feedback. Overall, our research provides a foundation for studying learning from digital feedback and demonstrates the potential for generalizing this learning to a variety of tasks. This study investigates how the advanced detection techniques used in CO-CPM, particularly CO-DCSK and CO-DCSK-II, improve performance in high-delay scenarios and explores the fundamental limitations of conventional differential detection methods. We examine various factors such as modulation order, phase shift levels, and symbol spacing to determine their impact on the optimal delay increase achievable through advanced detection techniques. To facilitate comparison, we also establish the optimal delay increase bounds for conventional differential detection methods. The results show that the new detection techniques can significantly enhance the acceptable delay in high-frequency fading channels by up to 512 times, far exceeding the limit of conventional techniques. To further illustrate the benefits of CO-DCSK, we present a prototype implementation of a wireless sensor network application using CO-DCSK and show that it outperforms the conventional differential detection method by an order of magnitude in terms of false alarm rate. The FFM consists of five broad dimensions: neuroticism, extraversion, openness to experience, agreeableness, and conscientiousness. By harnessing the predictive power of the FFM, healthcare systems can develop more effective and personalized strategies for reducing drug abuse and promoting healthy behaviors among individuals with various lifestyles and lifestyles aspirations. Our analysis revealed a distinct and country-independent pattern, where we could link certain personality traits to increased or decreased risk of drug abuse. For example, individuals with higher levels of neuroticism were more likely to be prescribed drugs with a higher abuse potential, such as opioids and sedatives, while individuals with higher levels of conscientiousness were less likely to be prescribed these drugs. Our proposed dataset, ATOMIC, is an exhaustive collection of common knowledge reasoning rules covering a wide range of topics.  Unlike other datasets that focus solely on factual information, ATOMIC is designed to facilitate reasoning about specific individuals or general topics.  Comprised of 157,109 diverse inference rules developed through human-machine interactions, ATOMIC demonstrates the potential for computational models to perform complex, abstract thinking.  Throughout our paper, we highlight the unique aspects of ATOMIC as well as its practical applications, ultimately showcasing the dataset's capacity to enhance the efficacy of generative models in multiple areas.  To further advance the field, we also introduce HumanCompletions -- a dataset of human-generated completion words for missing concepts in the abstract reasoning framework PrettyReason.  Through various evaluations, we both assess the performance of several state-of-the-art models on ATOMIC and explore the characteristics that contribute to the diversity within the dataset.  As a result, we contribute substantially to the development of the Abstract Reasoning for Machines research domain, provide valuable insights, and offer guidance for future work in this area.  Moreover, we make the HumanCompletions and PrettyReason datasets publicly available to facilitate further exploration of the underlying principles of computational reasoning.  Throughout the paper, we explore various topics such as the distinction between descriptive and prescriptive rules, the issue of potential bias within the dataset, and the challenge of evaluating the performance of models in an unbiased manner.  Ultimately, through both extensive human evaluations and rigorous automated assessments, we confirm the superiority of models trained with ATOMIC over their non-ATOMIC trained competitors in various challenges and tasks.  As a result, we provide strong evidence for the efficacy of large language models in learning to reason at the machine common knowledge level and set the stage for future advancements in this domain.  Additionally, we outline several potential applications across numerous areas such as natural language generation, by showcasing the capacity of models trained with ATOMIC to generate more coherent and meaningful text than their non-ATOMIC trained counterparts. Large-scale, high-performance linear algebra applications like scientific simulations and machine learning can benefit significantly from the O(N) linear scaling of the HHL quantum algorithm, particularly for large N. However, current Noisy Intermediate-Scale Quantum (NISQ) devices have limited qubit counts and high qubit losses, which hinder the practical implementation of HHL in its full, O(N) form. To overcome these challenges, we propose an extension to HHL known as NISQ-HHL, which involves breaking down large N matrices into smaller sub-matrices that can be processed on the available NISQ qubits. We examine various portfolio strategies for optimizing the distribution of qubits across these sub-matrices, taking into account the trade-off between qubit count, operation depth, and required qubit runtime for each sub-matrix. Our results show that focusing on minimizing total qubit runtime yields the most effective solution, but this involves complex optimization that can be challenging to execute on limited NISQ resources. As such, we introduce a novel, more manageable solution called the Qubit Recurrence Index (QRI), which can be calculated locally on the NISQ device and provides a straightforward, effective way to prioritize the processing of sub-matrices. When applied to various benchmark scenarios, NISQ-HHL exhibits significant improvements in execution time, often by several orders of magnitude, and significantly enhances the capability of current NISQ devices to perform linear algebra tasks on large N matrices. Moreover, we observe that in many instances, the overall scalability of NISQ-HHL is poised to break the qubit-count barrier, offering the potential for linear or even sublinear scaling in the number of qubits available. The development of larger-scale quantum processors with better qubit coherence and larger NISQ boxes will further accelerate the performance gains of NISQ-HHL. Additionally, we find that HHL applications can benefit from the integration of classical approximate matrix techniques, such as randomized iterative algorithms, and that our portfolio framework can be adapted to account for the effects of quantum errors, including the implementation of corrective retractions. The advancements made in this work will contribute to the development of quantum software that can take advantage of the unique capabilities of quantum processors, particularly in the near term. We introduce a novel multi-modal training framework that addresses these challenges. The proposed framework prevents the ASR model from relying solely on speech signals during training by introducing a second pathway that allows the model to process both speech and text simultaneously. This forces the model to extract more informative features from the speech signal. Additionally, our framework includes an attention mechanism that enables the model to allocate more attention to the speech signal when processing speech and text jointly. We evaluate our proposed framework on the TIMIT dataset and achieve significant improvements in ASR performance compared to standard multi-modal training methods. Furthermore, our approach requires no additional unlabeled speech data or specialized front-end extractors. We also explore the applicability of our proposed framework to large-scale ASR datasets and discuss potential future research directions for our framework. In the context of a perfect fluid, we investigate the inelastic scattering cross-section of a high-energy parton moving through a quark-gluon medium. This analysis highlights the influence of the medium on the parton's wave function, effectively modifying its scattering properties. By comparing the rates of inelastic scattering and the elastic scattering of a high-energy parton in a finite medium, we find that inelastic processes significantly enhance the imaginary part of the forward scattering amplitude, which may lead to an increased rate of parton energy loss and modified jet structure in heavy-ion collisions. Furthermore, we observe that the inelastic cross-section is dominated by the splitting of the parton into a heavy quark and a gluon, which dominates the medium's effect on the parton at finite temperature and density. This result suggests that the quark-gluon plasma exhibits characteristics more akin to a gluon-dominated medium than a fermionic one. Finally, we find that the inelastic cross-section is directly proportional to the square of the parton's color charge and is independent of its flavor and mass. This research is relevant to ongoing and future experiments that will be sensitive to the in-depth structure of quark-gluon plasmas. Additionally, our study is pertinent to the broader understanding of a parton's behavior within complex environments. Furthermore, our findings are expected to be validated across various models describing the properties of quark-gluon plasmas, which will be corroborated through comparisons with experimental data from heavy-ion collisions. This expertise hurdle hinders security audits, as well as cloud and containerized deployments, where ease of use and minimal operator requirements are expected. To address this challenge, we propose an innovative approach, inspired by programmatic configuration concepts, which leverages declarative specifications to automate the setup process. This approach is superior to imperative scripts, as it ensures consistent installations across different machines, eliminates the need for low-level command familiarity, and facilitates seamless integration with optimization and scaling tools. Our solution, called Treadmill, is an open-source, automated setup tool that employs declarative specifications and templating to streamline the setup process for distributed systems, including Hadoop and Spark clusters, cloud deployments, and virtual machine environments. By providing a clear specification language and a flexible templating mechanism, Treadmill enables the creation of custom declarative specifications tailored to specific system configurations, facilitating effortless installation of development tools, development environments, and other complex systems with numerous dependencies. Originally designed for setting up distributed transaction management systems, the Tephra installer now employs the same declarative specifications used by the Treadmill installer. In a previous series of experiments, we discovered how sticking forces changed as the temperature increased in a laboratory setup mimicking a planet-forming disk. To further expand this investigation, we conducted additional experiments under the same conditions, except this time we raised the temperature more gradually in the laboratory, to keep it below the point of complete sticking at 370 K. This more gradual increase was designed to better reflect the slower temperature rise experienced in an actual planet-forming disk. In the new series of experiments, we focused specifically on how sticking forces behaved when the temperature rose in two different types of test materials, one made of silicate glass particles and the other with added water, forming a glass-alumina-water mixture. We found that when we raised the temperature more gradually in the laboratory, the silicate glass particles showed a greater than expected rise in sticking forces at 360 K, followed by a decrease at 370 K. In contrast, the glass-alumina-water mixture exhibited a more gradual and linear increase in sticking forces as the temperature rose. This means that when temperatures reach 360 K, the silicate glass particles could potentially stick together at a rate 30 times faster than at 290 K, while the water-enriched test materials would stick together 7 times faster. This distinction in sticking behavior has significant implications for the development of planetary bodies, suggesting that any particles formed in a planet-forming disk with temperatures above 360 K would likely stick together quickly, forming larger particles, while particles in regions with lower temperatures would require more time to merge. Furthermore, this difference in sticking forces could also create a dividing line within a planet-forming disk, with inner regions favoring the formation of larger glass-alumina-water particles and outer regions forming larger silicate glass particles. This distinct breakdown of particle compositions could, in turn, influence the overall structure and composition of planetary bodies. Additionally, we discovered that any water present in the test materials not only accelerated sticking forces at elevated temperatures but also formed a bond that could withstand more force before breaking, implying that volatiles play a crucial role in sticking forces and may need to be reevaluated in models of planet formation. This, in turn, could alter our understanding of how planetary bodies form and grow in a planet-forming disk. Furthermore, this research may also provide valuable insights for other fields, such as the formation of dust particles in cometary atmospheres, dust deposition in asteroid belts, and the creation of dust shields in planetary systems. We designed an advanced computer vision approach known as YOLOv3, a real-time object detection algorithm, to efficiently identify binary asteroids within vast image collections, particularly those from the Pan-STARRS1 survey. Traditionally, detecting such binary phenomena requires precise positioning and measurement of the effects on an asteroid's brightness as it rotates. However, incorporating astronomical context into YOLOv3 enables it to prioritize certain features over others, thus potentially pinpointing binary asteroids within massive image datasets. We trained the YOLOv3 network on 135 known binary asteroids and 135 random single asteroids from the Pan-STARRS1 archive, utilizing 2048x2048 pixel images that encompass the asteroids' full diameter. We then tested the network's ability to detect these binary and single asteroids solely from their appearance within pan-STARRS1 historical images, without relying on brightness measurements. The results show that YOLOv3's accuracy surpasses that of human experts, correctly identifying 84% of binary and 78% of single asteroids. This model can be used to scan vast image collections more efficiently than traditional methods, potentially expanding the current list of known binary asteroids. We also explored the limitations of YOLOv3 in astronomical images, particularly its tendency to mistake single asteroids with small moons as binary targets, and identified potential strategies to address this in future research. The advanced computer vision techniques we explored have the potential to be adapted to other astronomical object detection applications. Additionally, we discovered that combining YOLOv3 with existing data on asteroid properties and astronomical contexts can be done through a feature extractor layer, thereby integrating computer vision approaches with existing astronomical databases. This is the first study in which a deep convolutional neural network was used to identify binary asteroids solely from their appearance within historical image collections. YOLOv3's ability to scan vast image collections more efficiently than traditional methods makes it a valuable tool for the astronomical community. This research is also an example of how transferring general-purpose computer vision algorithms to other domains can be beneficial. Furthermore, we demonstrated that high-performance object detection algorithms like YOLOv3 can be used in science-driven applications, and we successfully integrated a neural network with an astronomical database on asteroid properties and contexts. This is a unique combination that could also be applied to other astronomical object detection problems. The Southern Atlantic ridge is the gentlest and most slowly moving mid-ocean ridge, extending approximately 8,500 km from 20°N to 34°50'S latitude.  It features a central rift valley with numerous offset fissures, most notable being the St. Helena, Walvis, and Rio Grande rifts.  A thorough analysis of the kinematics within the southern segment of the Atlantic ridge was conducted by examining transform offsets, fault systems, and migration patterns of the fissures.  This study found that the southern Atlantic ridge features non-linear and asymmetrical kinematics, with distinct variations observed across different sections.  Results indicate that the Southern Atlantic ridge moveses at a pace of 15-20 km/Ma in the south, but its fissure system exhibits evidence of first-order simplification, suggesting that this ridge has maintained its overall geometry for at least the past 80 million years.  This study also discovered that the Rio Grande and Walvis rifts are migrating at a rate of 5-6 cm/yr, while the St. Helena rift is stationary.  Analysis of the seismic data along the southern Atlantic ridge revealed a zone of seismicity along its axis, but it surprisingly did not show any evidence of repeating patterns of seismic activity.  This study further found that the southern Atlantic ridge features a system of non-repeating, en-echelon, right-lateral faults that accommodate about 70% of the ridge's sea-floor spreading, while the remaining 30% is taken up by the migration of the fissures.  This unique fault system of the southern Atlantic ridge is thought to result from the ridge's unique geometry and low magmatic budget, characterized by large, shallow magma chambers.  This study also offers new explanations for the observed variations across different sections of the southern Atlantic ridge, its unique geometry, and the patterns of seismic activity and spreading axes that shift over time.  This study further provides a new model that can be applicable to other mid-ocean ridges. This study's outcome has also confirmed that the southern Atlantic ridge's unique features result from this ridge having reached a state of equilibrium with its low magmatic budget, a condition that this study believes is also applicable to other mid-ocean ridges. A prominent approach in medical image segmentation is deep learning, particularly through segmentation networks that leverage image information to produce masks. However, training these networks with high accuracy requires a large set of labeled data, which is often expensive and difficult to obtain for many medical applications. A alternative strategy is to use a two-network system: one main network is trained to segment images based on input images alone, without labels, while a second auxiliary network is used to optimize the main network's performance using the generated segmentations. We propose a novel boundary-sensitive loss function that can be integrated into this approach. By minimizing this loss, the main network is forced to produce masks with accurate boundary information, which is critical in medical image segmentation. We also explore various modifications to this loss function and verify the effectiveness of our proposed strategy through self-supervised training on a public renal tumor segmentation dataset. The results demonstrate its superiority over alternative methods. Furthermore, we find that modifying the auxiliary network's loss function to prioritize interior information can be beneficial, especially in scenarios with poorly defined tumor boundaries. We introduce the first known application of a machine learning model in the realm of tabletop gaming, specifically in Dungeons and Dragons. This involves training an automated Dungeon Master using natural language processing, which can create environments for two players to engage in role-playing activities. We develop a set of techniques to teach the automated Dungeon Master to understand player intentions and create scenarios accordingly, all within a pre-defined world framework defined by player goals and a game map. This capability is referred to as a Theory-of-Mind for the Dungeon Master, which can be learned through player interactions and refined over time, allowing the automated Dungeon Master to craft more challenging and coherent scenarios and better manage the pace of the game. When compared to a non-learning-based approach and one alternative method, our proposed method results in higher scores from human evaluators in aspects such as natural language use and overall game enjoyment. Additionally, this method's ability to understand player thoughts and incorporate them into the story creates a more immersive and responsive gaming experience. All code and data used in this study are now available on GitHub. This research is a significant step in exploring the potential of machine learning in supporting and collaborating with humans in creative, interactive activities. We hope this work will be of use to developers of automated Dungeon Master tools and anyone interested in the intersection of artificial intelligence and gaming. Three important research questions emerge from this study: (1) What other methods can be developed to train automated Dungeon Masters using various machine learning techniques? (2) How can we ensure the stories created by automated Dungeon Masters are coherent and meaningful? (3) What other applications can Theory-of-Mind for multi-agent interactions have in areas like human-autonomous vehicle collaboration and emotional intelligence? Despite significant research, identifying semantic shifts in word meanings remains a challenging task. Many studies have linked this difficulty to the limited size of current lexical resources, which fail to capture the nuances of word meanings due to substantial knowledge bases. Furthermore, existing methods primarily focus on analyzing individual words in isolation, neglecting the complex network of word relationships and nuances of word meanings, particularly in domains with specialized vocabularies. This paper proposes an innovative approach, combining neural-based word representation with semantic analysis, to accurately track the evolution of word meanings within a given text corpus. By leveraging the structure of the vocabulary, this method enhances the discovery of hidden semantic shifts by incorporating multiple words at once. To validate this approach, extensive experiments were conducted on three publicly available datasets, and the results show substantial improvements over state-of-the-art techniques. Furthermore, this paper explores the fundamental question of what constitutes a semantic shift in word meanings by examining the internal structure of the word embeddings to provide a preliminary answer, along with a practical solution to identify such shifts. The proposed framework also facilitates the creation of a comprehensive lexical resource that maps words to their semantic meanings and tracks the evolution of these meanings across a corpus. This new framework outperforms existing methods on the task of semantic shift detection and sheds light on the internal structure of the word embeddings, a topic that until now had not been extensively studied. The accompanying code and the newly created LexicoSemShifts dataset are available for download at https://github.com/AndreaBorillo/SemShifts. This work has important implications for the development of more sophisticated lexical resources and the enhancement of natural language understanding models. Furthermore, the results of this research can be applied to the development of advanced applications such as word sense induction tools and specialized search engines with a high level of precision. The intricate relationship between protein knots and their functional potential has sparked significant interest in the field. Building upon our previous research, we've developed a computational approach that leverages topological rules to systematically analyze the native state structures of proteins. By applying this method to a vast library of knotted proteins, our results reveal a surprising pattern: a significant proportion of these proteins are linked by a relatively small number of low-index cross-links, which we term the "universal decoupling set". Furthermore, we've found that almost every knotted protein structure can be efficiently unraveled into a much simpler state characterized by just a few of these low-index crossings. These findings leaped forward to the next layer, where we examine the spatial arrangements of amino acids within these unfolded states. By comparing the sequences of these unfolded states to their corresponding folded counterparts, we've identified a clear correlation between the structure of these unfolded states and the specific locations of peptide loops in the protein chain. Moreover, we've established a clear distinction between two main categories of these unfolded states, which we've termed "bending pathways" and "loop-crossing pathways". While loop-crossing pathways are shown to prevent the passage of a non-abiding knot, bending pathways are shown to allow for the resolution of knots through loop rearrangements. Interestingly, a significant proportion of these unfolding paths correspond to low-index cross-links in the universal decoupling set. Additionally, we've discovered that many knotted proteins share common unfolding paths, which are often related to the protein's functional role. By exploring the relationship between these unfolding paths and the local chemical properties of the protein, we've identified patterns that could be exploited in the design of novel enzymes. Finally, we demonstrate the practical utility of our approach by applying it to the creation of a novel enzyme based on the rules governing its sequence and structure. This novel enzyme, optimized for the efficient hydrolysis of a glycogen substrate, outperforms its natural counterpart in the optimal condition we defined through our computations. This breakthrough was made possible by our ability to accurately predict the Loewenstein interaction energies and pKa values of specific amino acid positions within the enzyme's active site. Building upon our findings, we propose a general framework for the rational design of novel enzymes by incorporating their folding patterns and unfolding pathways. This predictive approach could be expanded to address more complex challenges in protein engineering, such as loop rearrangements and the stabilization of protein structures. A detailed investigation into the Nambu-Goldstone (NG) boson phenomenon has been launched, with an emphasis on its underlying theoretical mechanisms. Both relativistic and nonrelativistic quantum field theories are examined as part of this study. The process involves analyzing a generic SU(Nc) gauge theory's vacuum structure and evaluating the properties of NG bosons within a general framework. A systematic explanation of the conditions that favor NG boson presence is then provided. Furthermore, generalizations of the 't Hooft automatic theorem, which states that a spontaneous symmetry breaking results in the presence of NG bosons, are also identified. A new classification of the 't Hooft automatic theorem is proposed, with distinct components, including the original form, as well as two additional scenarios: one where the symmetry is not fully broken, or where it is broken without a massless particle appearing as a consequence. A key contribution of this research is the proposal of an even more comprehensive framework for the 't Hooft automatic theorem, which is supported by both relativistic and nonrelativistic quantum field theory. Prior research revealed constraints based on data sets used for training, but more analysis is needed to understand the fundamental capabilities of these models in producing counterfactuals. We introduce the first evaluation framework called DISCO, designed to assess a model's capacity to generate counterfactuals, and conduct comprehensive experiments to examine the performance of various LLM architectures when generating counterfactuals. Our results show that boosting a model's counterfactual ability is dependent on increasing the diversity of training data, with surprisingly little improvement observed from upgrading to larger models despite expected gains. Analyzing generated counterfactuals with quantitative and qualitative methods offers further insights into the limitations and constraints of LLMs in producing counterfactuals. Our research discovers that generating counterfactuals is a biased process with regards to syntax and semantics, and several restrictions on the form and content of counterfactuals must be followed. The findings from this study have important implications for the development of next-generation language models with counterfactual capabilities. The flow of an ideal polymer solution through a narrow channel is examined in relation to its viscosity behavior. Contrary to conventional polymer flow which degrades over time due to shear thinning, ideal polymers maintain their viscosity properties. This unique property causes viscosity to increase linearly with time while the polymer is present, leading to a grinding force that slows fluid velocity. As a result, the fraction of space occupied by the polymer plug becomes a constant over time. It follows that the shape of the polymer plug changes from a sharp front to a cumulative distribution similar to the Gaussian distribution. Traditionally, machine learning algorithms are tested and evaluated using thoroughly annotated training data. Nonetheless, in practice, obtaining such extensive annotations can be very expensive. A more cost-effective approach involves using single positive labels for each instance, indicating that the instance should be included in a specific category. In this research, we contend that in such scenarios, the usual binary classification framework is inadequate and propose a novel multi-label extraction model. Specifically, we suggest that the gamma-rays could be the result of gamma-ray production when electrons in the jet interact with the magnetic field in a disk of matter that has accumulated as a result of the star being magnetically drawn in. We develop a quantitative model that takes into account various factors such as the brightness of the galaxy's radio emission, the rate at which matter is drawn into the disk, and the strength of the magnetic field. Applying our model to several nearby radio galaxies, we found that it is capable of explaining the observed levels of very-high-energy gamma-ray emission. Additionally, our model predicts the existence of detectable levels of gamma-ray emission in over a hundred nearby radio galaxies.
