The approach developed in this paper addresses this challenge for arrangements of lines in a two-dimensional space, and it demonstrates that an unknown binary string can be reliably reconstructed from a set of user feedback with a high probability, provided that the number of possible locations for a point in the arrangement exceeds the Hamming distance between the binary code and a specific binary alphabet. The theoretical analysis and the results from numerous computer simulations support the validity of this approach. Furthermore, this paper proposes an new algorithm for calculating the number of points in an arrangement of lines, and it showcases the effectiveness of a simple user recruitment strategy for the underlying problem. It also provides a general framework for (not necessarily cryptographic) applications that involve anonymous interactions between users, and it highlights the arrangements of hyperplanes as a valuable tool for their system design. Finally, it presents several open research questions related to both cryptography and arrangements of hyperplanes. Classifying musical instruments using audio clips is a challenge that has been addressed using various machine learning techniques, yet many methods fall short in achieving high accuracy for unknown instruments. One significant limitation hindering progress in this area is the scarcity of comprehensive databases that cover a broad range of instruments. To overcome this obstacle, we propose a novel approach, centered around a hierarchical framework called the "Taxonomic Neural Adapter" (TNA), which leverages a basic prototype network and adapts to target instruments within a predefined taxonomy. By doing so, the TNA can efficiently recognize families of instruments even with minimal expert annotation. To evaluate the TNA's performance, we introduce the "Instrument Family Hierarchy" (IFIH) - a comprehensive taxonomy spanning 12 categories and 96 instruments, along with 2000 annotated clips available for research purposes. Through a suite of experiments, the TNA consistently outperformed baseline models, showcasing the TNA's potential as a versatile and adaptable solution for a wide range of musical instrument identification tasks. The code and datasets used in this research may be found at https://github.com/andersonbrito/taxonomic-neural-adapter. Acronyms and abbreviations serve as shorter versions of lengthy phrases, commonly found across diverse writing mediums. While they are instrumental in saving space and time in written communication, they also introduce comprehension hurdles if not clearly defined, particularly if the acronym's origin is unclear in lengthy texts. To address this, numerous approaches to automatic acronym identification and resolution have been attempted but thus far, effectively handling real-world scenarios remains a challenge. This research endeavors to present a pioneering, user-interfaced system, MadDog, devised to accurately pinpoint and interpret acronyms in ordinary language. MadDog's underlying framework, built using a range of natural language processing techniques, includes an acronym recognition module, a word pattern recognition system, and a database of commonly used acronyms. To evaluate MadDog's performance, we assembled a comprehensive acronym database, dubbed MadDog's Knowledge Base, Accessible via the MadDog website. User-interaction with the system is facilitated through a user-friendly interface available at http://www.cs.umb.edu/~jim/MadDog/. System documentation, including technical details and user guidelines, is available for download from the same website. Experimental studies with MadDog have yielded promising results, and we anticipate that the system, with its user-centric approach, will contribute meaningfully to the acronyms domain. Additionally, we hope that MadDog's knowledge base will evolve into a comprehensive acronym database, beneficial for numerous applications. This research paper is an extension of our earlier publication, presented at the 2009 International Conference on Advances in Artificial Intelligence (ICAI09). Key innovations introduced in this expanded version of the paper include MadDog's design philosophy, the system's architecture, and a detailed analysis of its performance. Furthermore, we have incorporated feedback from numerous acronyms-related research studies published since ICAI09. This enhanced version of MadDog has been successfully validated with real-world inputs, and its upgraded database now encompasses over 2000 entries. Topological insulators represent a significant phenomenon in modern physics research, characterized by robust nodal surfaces in momentum space that protect against gapping. In this paper, we examine the diverse forms these nodal surfaces can take, discussing their topological origins and common manifestations in momentum-space representations. We also review recent efforts to create artificial topological systems in optics and other fields, using metamaterials and other techniques that can engineer nodal surfaces within parametric space. By bringing together theoretical concepts and experimental developments, this work showcases the value of modeling real-space phenomena using momentum-space frameworks, and highlights potential for further breakthroughs in topological research. Additionally, we explore the broader implications of studying topological systems through momentum-space nodal surfaces, emphasizing their relation to other fundamental ideas like symmetry protection and wave packet dynamics. We conclude by highlighting the most promising directions for future topological research, including time-topological insulators, and the use of momentum-space constructs as abstract frameworks for understanding complex phenomena. We anticipate this review will provide a useful starting point for researchers looking to enter the expanding field of topological physics. Currently available medical image computing methods are not effectively identifying and classifying brain tumors from MRI scans. To address this challenge, researchers have been using deep learning techniques such as convolutional neural networks (CNN). However, applying such methods is complicated due to limited access to labeled datasets, particularly for certain tumor types. To overcome these obstacles and improve the accuracy of brain tumor detection and classification, we've developed a multi-task directed network called MAG-Net. This novel framework is designed to efficiently process a large number of images from various sources, including ClincicalACR and MICCAI challenge datasets, without needing extensive labeled data for specific tumor types. By utilizing pre-trained models and a set of basic, easily identifiable features such as edges and regions, MAG-Net can effectively identify and classify brain tumors from MRI scans. The network's structure, known as a multi-task directed graph, allows it to prioritize certain tasks over others for each input image, thereby minimizing unnecessary computations and memory usage. Through extensive experiments using Open-source Brain tumor Recognition Frameworks (BOBFRs), MAG-Net demonstrated superior performance in tumor segmentation and classification from low-to-high difficulty levels, with results surpassing those of existing approaches and a notable gain in efficient use of computational resources. Reconstructing 3D scenes from 2D images fails when dealing with shadows, which can now be addressed using an innovative method that calculates shadow casting exactly, even in complex environments, using a combination of techniques such as differentiable ray tracing, volumetric rendering, and optimization. This approach makes shadow handling consistent and efficient, compared to existing piecemeal methods, and significantly improves the accuracy of scene reconstruction. Moreover, it enables the learning of end-to-end differentiable dark matter models, which can detect and remove shadows, leading to enhanced results in image-based applications, such as deblurring, inpainting, and image enhancement, without specifically targeting those tasks. This research introduces an executable shadow evaluation module, a shadow-oriented dark path optimization formula, and a differentiable shadow mask generator, which can be incorporated into popular 3D reconstruction and shading frameworks. Experiments demonstrate the superiority of this approach over conventional methods and existing solutions proposed in recent research. This technique has been implemented and the code is available online at https://github.com/zwang84/ExactShadowEval. This research was conducted under the guidance of Prof. Huanjing Zhu, Prof. Liang-Zhen Wang, and Prof. Huaibin Wang at the Xi'an Jiaotong University in China. This research paper will be presented at the CVPR 2021 conference in virtual format due to travel restrictions.

A popular technique in video processing, lacing-based video enhancement can transform low-quality video captured from far, recording a wide angle, or with rolling shutter effects into a more clear and distortion-free version. This task poses specific challenges: enhancing the picture while maintaining the original size and frame rate, and rectifying distracting rolling shutter distortions along with motion blurs. We present a novel approach to achieve this goal, a deep learning-based model, where a specially designed filter eliminates distortion during training, and we demonstrate its effectiveness with two primary scenarios: deinterlacing single frames and entire video clips. Our method outperforms existing competitors, producing results with minimal artifacts and superior quality. Our code is readily available online at https://github.com/hjdw/InstantDeepVideoDeinterlacing. We have also included extensive experimental evaluations, along with a comprehensive comparison against other top-performing deep deinterlacing models. Our results show that our proposed approach consistently yields the best subjective and objective performance. We have used a wide range of real-world videos to test our method's performance, and the accompanying movie can be found at https://youtu.be/9O9sDdZLd3Y. Our research demonstrates the potential of deep learning to tackle complex video processing challenges. We have further explored applications of our model in video super-resolution and video deraining. These experiments indicate that a pre-trained deep deinterlacing model can be repurposed with only minimal retraining for video enhancement tasks. We have also analyzed the role of different convolutional neural network components in deep deinterlacing. We have identified key factors that contribute to a neural network's ability to learn interlacing patterns and the efficient processing of rolling shutter distortions. We have used these insights to design a compact state-of-the-art neural network, capable of processing even large-scale video frames with rolling shutter distortions. This model's efficiency makes it an ideal choice for real-time video deinterlacing applications. We have experimented with a vast collection of 2D and 3D convolutional neural network architectures, carefully evaluating each one based on its performance. We have selected the best deep deinterlacing model from our experiments and further optimized its design. We have achieved significant improvements over the existing state-of-the-art methods with our proposed deep deinterlacing model. We have validated the generalization performance of our model on unseen test datasets and real-world videos. We have analyzed the motion blur correction capability of our deep deinterlacing model through extensive experiments.

This study evaluates the square radius of the neutron distribution, defined as <r_2>, within the framework of average field models. Our examination covers both relativistic and non-relativistic approaches, with specific examples including the Relativistic Mean Field model and the Non-Relativistic Mean Field model. Our analysis indicates that the choice of theoretical framework significantly influences the calculated value of <r_2>. For neutrons in the double magic nucleus 120Sn, the predicted <r_2> values vary substantially, with estimates ranging from approximately 47 fm^2 to over 50 fm^2. Our analysis also highlights that experimental measurements of <r_2> are currently insufficient to distinguish between theoretical predictions. Nevertheless, given that theoretical models can diverge in their <r_2> predictions even for basic nuclear properties, further experimental advancements are necessary for a more comprehensive understanding of neutron distribution. This study is a follow-up to our earlier investigation focused on the charge density distribution, where we found similar discrepancies among theoretical predictions. Collective analysis of both proton and neutron distribution radii may provide valuable insights into the underlying characteristics of average field models. Given the significance of <r_2> in low-energy nuclear physics and the related properties such as electric dipole moments, our study encourages a re-examination of existing and potential future experimental measurements of <r_2> to refine our understanding of average field models. Furthermore, it highlights the value of a re-evaluation of existing data in light of new theoretical predictions. Our analysis also highlights that the predicted <r_2> values are highly dependent on the specific average field model employed, with substantial variations arising from the different treatment of the Dirac masses within the Relativistic Mean Field model. This distinction may serve as an indicator for the choice of most appropriate average field model. Our analysis also suggests that the predicted <r_2> values may serve as a criterion for the evaluation of different average field models. This is particularly relevant given the widespread use of average field models in research and the significance of <r_2> in low-energy nuclear physics. Precise and efficient river flow velocity predictions are crucial for various applications such as managing flood risks. While the shallow water equations are commonly employed for this purpose, their traditional numerical solutions can be time-consuming and require precise riverbed measurements. In this research, a non-traditional approach is tested where the flow velocities are predicted directly from point measurements using machine learning algorithms, specifically leveraging virtual spatial nodes with optimized contributions weighted by the distance from the measurement point. This research evaluates two potential models: one using a fixed number of virtual nodes and another where the number of virtual nodes is determined automatically. The former was found to significantly improve the performance compared to standard kriging and neural network predictors, while the latter showed potential benefits but required more exploration. The approach was successfully applied to actual river flow data. Furthermore, a key aspect of this research was the use of a deep learning algorithm called Neural Network Filter to preprocess the data, remove outliers, and prepare it for prediction. This approach resulted in accurate predictions of river flow velocities compared to reference solutions obtained from the shallow water equations, with an average error of 0.14 m/s. The code for this project has been made publicly available on the GitHub repository https://github.com/laetgil/RiverFlow-Prediction. The protocol for the machine learning approach has also been included in the code, enabling replication of the results. The website https://riverflow-prediction.com provides an interactive interface for users to input river flow velocity measurement data and receive predictions of flow velocities at desired locations. The data used in this research was based on river flow velocities measured every 10 minutes over a year in three Korean rivers, with further details available in the appendix. The predictions generated by this model were validated against actual river flow velocities measured every hour over a period of three years, with the average error reaching 0.048 m/s. The research demonstrates the potential of machine learning to accurately predict river flow velocities from point measurements, offering a rapid and efficient alternative to traditional numerical solutions of the shallow water equations. The findings have been shared with the Korean government, prompting plans to implement this approach in the country's flood risk management system. The research has also been recognized with an award from the Korean Ministry of Science and Technology at the 2022 International Conference on Artificial Intelligence in Music, Performance, and Visual Arts. The paper has been published in the journal Advances in Artificial Intelligence (2022). The award recognizes the innovative application of artificial intelligence in displaying the results of river flow velocity predictions, as showcased in the paper

The successful application of an efficient heat transfer technique, rapid heating, depends on a clear understanding of temperature distributions within both solid and gas phases of a bed. This study utilizes a novel MRI technique to map temperature changes in a horizontal sand bed infused with air flowing upward, a configuration known as a "dune" structure. By rapidly increasing the temperature at the bottom of the sand bed, a temperature difference of up to 100 K is created across the sand layer. The resulting temperature maps indicate that the temperature variation along the height of the dune increases nonlinearly, presenting potential challenges for models aiming to predict fully developed thermal patterns. The discovery of temperature differences within the dune, particularly the phenomenon of "temperature fingers," warrants further examination of the flow patterns and the development of more comprehensive heat transfer models. The proposed MRI method offers a versatile temperature mapping technique with broad applications across various bed types and flow rates, making it an ideal tool for researchers in the fields of geophysics and chemical engineering. The data and insights gathered from this study are also relevant to the optimization of heat transfer processes in fluidized beds and the development of numerical models for such processes. The utility of the presented MRI temperature mapping approach is demonstrated by its successful application to (1) obtaining experimental data for model validation, (2) analyzing flow patterns, and (3) developing more accurate models of heat transfer. The technical innovations presented in this study have the potential to contribute to the development of more effective heat transfer techniques and the better understanding of phenomena in porous media. The novel MRI temperature mapping method presented in this study takes advantage of the high sensitivity of proton spin-lattice relaxation to temperature changes and utilizes a rapid imaging sequence to obtain temperature maps from the intensity of MRI images. The accuracy of this method is validated by comparing the temperature measurements to those obtained from a high-precision thermometer. The temperature resolution of this approach is found to be reliable at the $2/K$ level over the measured temperature range. The novel MRI temperature mapping approach is a versatile technique that can be adapted to various types of beds and is suitable for both low- and high-temperature measurements. The recent integration of this method with the use of superconducting quantum magnets has significantly improved the speed of temperature mapping. Unfortunately, the traditional approach to uncertainty analysis, based on probability theory, has limitations when dealing with open-world uncertainties in modern critical systems. In contrast, our novel uncertainty modeling framework builds upon the concept of energies as costs, a theoretical foundation that underpins the success of formal verification and assurance cases. By leveraging this framework, we demonstrate its effectiveness in addressing open-world uncertainties by example, particularly in the development of safety-critical systems. Our uncertainty modeling framework disability-specific energy functions can handle the complexities of the socio-technical systems, such as cyber-physical systems, whereas its combination with the assurance-calibration framework for uncertainty, named ACCUTE, addresses the challenge of scalability. ACCUTE's key features, including adjustable precision via energy levels and validated at-design and at-run-time performance, make it an ideal choice for the rapid development of safety-critical systems. Our research on ACCUTE underscores the potential of the energy-driven open-world uncertainty modeling framework to revolutionize the development of safety-critical systems through the rapid assurance-calibration of uncertainties. Furthermore, we introduce a novel metric, called assurance confidence, that provides a systematic approach to evaluating and comparing different solutions. By exploring real-world applications and a benchmark dataset, we confirm the superiority of solutions with higher assurance confidence when compared to those with lower or no confidence. Our research on the assurance-confidence metric reveals its effectiveness in pinpointing the optimal solution, reducing the search-space by an average of three orders of magnitude. Lastly, our research on both the uncertainty modeling framework and the metric highlights the value of interdisciplinarity, the integration of computer science and physics. Through our research, we demonstrate how the assurance-confidence metric can be used to address the challenge of uncertainty quantification head-on. Furthermore, we explore an exciting area of research, centered on the interdisciplinarity of computer science and physics, by introducing a new paradigm for the development of safety-critical systems. Through our research, we introduce the concept of co-design, an innovative approach to the development of safety-critical systems that involves the simultaneous design of both the system's hardware and software. Despite notable breakthroughs in reinforcement learning, numerous significant hurdles remain when applying it to dynamic and ever-changing problems common in critical domains, including robotics and complex gameplay. Reinforcement learning models generally struggle to generalize effectively when confronted with new tasks beyond their training data. In response to this challenge, the field is seeing an increased focus on continual learning methods, and to support this research, new tools are being developed, including carefully crafted evaluation environments and benchmark tasks. To address this need, we present Lifelong Learning Explorer (L2Explorer), an intuitive, interactive environment that allows evaluation of lifelong learning strategies in complex, dynamic worlds. L2Explorer is designed to be user-friendly and adaptable to various application areas, including both simulated and real-world robotics scenarios, as well as video game environments. Its key features include customizable world mappings, various types of transfer scenarios, and transparent observation and action definitions, making it easily accessible to both lifelong learning experts and non-experts. We also introduce Antipastos, a challenging set of tasks designed to evaluate the performance of lifelong learning algorithms in challenging, complex situations. Antipastos joins L2Explorer as a premier benchmark suite, and both the environment and the suite are available at https://l2explorer.org. By providing a free, community-driven platform for advancing lifelong learning research, we aim to create a resource that supports the development of new evaluation methods and cutting-edge lifelong learning techniques. Two notable approaches are presented in an exploratory capacity, including an exploration strategy and a novel application of a lifelong learning method, both of which are evaluated using L2Explorer and Antipastos. Their results demonstrate the effectiveness of both approaches in overcoming several key obstacles to successful lifelong learning. One of the proposed methods, for instance, successfully addresses the challenge of preventing learning performance from fluctuating when tackling new tasks, while the other yields superior performance when compared to traditional methods in critical domains, despite being trained with a significantly more limited dataset. These findings provide initial evidence for the validity of L2Explorer and Antipastos as evaluation tools and benchmarks, and both are being further developed as open-source projects with support from Google's Lifelong Learning Research Award. In response to the growing interest in lifelong learning, we believe that developing evaluation environments and benchmark tasks will continue to play a critical role in the development of new continuous learning approaches. As a practical application of this concept, we examine the scenario of super-resolving optical beam profiling through SMD in a two-field setup, and our results indicate that this approach can yield a level of performance that is several times better than the conventional diffraction limited resolution, even when the resolution is dominated by a Gaussian transmission function. Given the possibility that this event might be linked to the planet's interior, our research presents a contrasting theory, suggesting the temperature surge originated from angular momentum released in its molten core, rather than being absorbed from the planet's interior. This alternative explanation, supported by the planet's likely high equilibrium temperature and possibility of it having a highly resistant solid inner core, could also provide insight into its formation history. We introduce a novel approach called the Meta Neural Process Method, which leverages a suite of fact-checking models to recognize patterns across multiple data sources, including social media networks, blogs, and online forums. This work delves into Yang-Baxter operators associated with a specific type of finite set-theoretic solution to the Yang-Baxter equation and establish connections to quasi-bialgebras and quasi-hopf algebras. Specifically, we identify a subset of the solutions whose underlying set has a specific structure, and demonstrate that a particular type of Yang-Baxter operator, when associated with these solutions, results in a subalgebra whose properties include being a quasi-bialgebra and quasi-hopf algebra. Furthermore, we introduce the concept of "generic" solutions and their corresponding Yang-Baxter operators, and demonstrate that these generic solutions yield a specific type of Yang-Baxter operator that, when combined with the Yang-Baxter equation's symmetry property, produces a quasi-bialgebra whose definition is independent of the solution's permutation. Additionally, we explore various parameters and their effects on the Yang-Baxter operators and associated algebras, concluding that they either act as scalars or generators within the resulting algebras. Finally, we discuss potential applications of set-theoretic solutions to the Yang-Baxter equation in the study of quasi-bialgebras and quasi-hopf algebras. This research builds upon previous work by Gruenow and Militzer in "Set-theoretic solution classes of the Yang-Baxter equation and their associated Yang-Baxter operators" and establishes concrete connections between set-theoretic solutions to the Yang-Baxter equation and quasi-bialgebras. This is the first part of my PhD thesis, with the second part focusing on specific examples of set-theoretic solutions. The ultimate control of spin currents is dependent on the precise manipulation of valence electron dynamics.  In silicon, precise direction of the spin current can be challenging due to the inherent symmetry of the valence electron wave functions.  Recent studies have demonstrated the capability of directing the spin current in silicon by utilizing an atomic scale interface between silicon and hydrogen.  A newly discovered mechanism, one-dimensional Heisenberg spin coupling along the surface atomic array of H-Si bonds, offers a chance to overcome the difficulties associated with valence electron based control of spin currents.  The vector nature of the spin current can be understood by examining the angular momentum density distribution across the H-Si interface.  Furthermore, quasi one-dimensional hydrogen covered Si(110) surfaces exhibit unique atomic scale features that facilitate precise control of the spin current.  A newly described phenomenon, one-dimensional helical valley interference, opens up possibilities for highly precise control of the spin current.  These discoveries provide novel paths to achieving precise control of spin currents that could be beneficial for creating highly efficient spin transfer and magnetic recording technologies.  A model illustrating one-dimensional helical valley interference can be explained through a band structure model and a Heisenberg Hamiltonian.  However, more comprehensive studies are required to fully understand the underlying physics of these phenomena.  A potential research pathway could involve investigations into the effects of neighborhood variations on the one-dimensional Heisenberg coupling, verification of the predicted effects through higher-order Heisenberg Hamiltonians, and a broader examination of quasi one-dimensional systems through model development and application of group theory.  These studies could provide a deeper understanding of the physics behind valley interference and spin transfer and contribute to the development of novel spin transfer technologies.  Additionally, a broader exploration of the physics of atomic scale interfaces could give rise to innovative applications of the Heisenberg coupling in solid state systems.  In the context of silicon based quantum computing, the discovery of one-dimensional Heisenberg coupling could lead to the development of robust and scalable quantum processors through the incorporation of atomic scale interfaces in silicon.  Furthermore, the exploration of one-dimensional Heisenberg coupling could also contribute to the advancement of hydrogen based nanoengineering, a field that could benefit from a more in-depth understanding of the effects of neighborhood variations on Heisenberg coupling.  Ultimately, the broader exploration of the physics of atomic scale interfaces in silicon could give rise to innovative applications of the Heisenberg coupling in solid state systems, encompassing fields such as quantum computing, spin transfer technologies, and hydrogen based nanoengineering. The Understanding Dynamics and Framework of Complex Systems (UDICS) challenge focuses on developing an explanatory and predictive understanding of complex systems, particularly those with intricate and ever-changing components. It highlights the need to view a system's structure and interactions as interlinked, shifting paradigms, and emphasizes the importance of both temporal and structural knowledge in grasping the underlying mechanics of these systems. The UDICS competition aims to establish a benchmark for modeling complex systems using Graph Neural Networks (GNNs), with particular emphasis on two tasks: framework understanding and dynamic understanding. For the benchmark, the organizers chose three complex systems with publicly available data, including scientific collaborations, Wikipedia networks, and air transportation systems. The models are evaluated against human-annotated labels and are given access to extensive temporal training data. The organizers issued a technical report outlining the statistics and key findings from the competition, including the superior performance of meta-learning GNNs on the Wikipedia dataset, the success of simple GNNs on the scientific collaborations and air transportation systems, and the challenges posed by limited-label data and the absence of explicit temporal GNN benchmarks. The article also introduces the concept of multi-layer system architecture and presents a pioneering study on the architecture of Wikipedia through a UDICS-style GNN meta-learning framework. The results demonstrate the efficacy of meta-learning in discovering the underlying structure and dynamics of complex systems like Wikipedia, the identification of multiple layers in this architecture, and the learning of simple temporal mechanics in a real-world air transportation system. The article is an extension of the authors' previous work presented on Google Research Commons and the leaders' talk at the UDICS competition workshop at the 35th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2021). The total secure coordination mechanism outperformed existing approaches in terms of throughput and equalized the processing load among participating astrobots. GP 2 is a graph-based language designed for efficient program analysis and verification, leveraging graph transformation rules to ease these tasks. However, efficiently developing and utilizing GP 2 programs poses significant challenges, primarily resulting from the complex dependencies inherent to graph transformations. To overcome these obstacles for programs targeting GP 2's machine language, known as GPM, we have developed an optimized GP 2 compiler called GP 4. This compiler optimizes program execution by: minimizing unnecessary graph modifications; avoiding expensive rule applications; eliminating redundant computations; and prioritizing rule executions based on likely program behavior. To achieve these improvements, GP 4 employs an array of innovative techniques, such as: (1) pre-analyzing and optimizing program modules; (2) dynamically classifying and optimizing graph states during execution; (3) dynamically optimizing the availability of program components; (4) predicting and guiding the behavior of graph transformations; (5) leveraging user-provided information for optimization; and (6) dynamically managing and reconfiguring the compiler's optimization strategies. By integrating these techniques, GP 4 significantly enhances GP 2's performance, outperforming a naive GP 2 interpreter while delivering up to 104 times faster execution for benchmark programs. The GP 4 compiler offers its optimization strategies in the form of the Enhanced GP 2 (EGP 2) front-end, which can be utilized as a compiler framework for programming languages based on graph transformation, such as GPM. The EGP 2 framework, along with its compiler, is available at https://github.com/EnhancedGP2. Additionally, we have created an interactive visualization tool for visualizing the behavior of GP 2 programs, graph states, and the classification of graph transformations, all of which can be found at https://enhancedgp2.org. This research focuses on automated panoramic image stitching, a task where a camera rotates to capture scenes and then produces a panoramic image by combining the taken pictures. The problem is significant in various areas like astronomy, where the rotation allows for the capture of wider scenes, and the stitching of the images can also be used to create more comprehensive astronomical maps. The new method is also more robust than existing astronomical stitching methods, which do not account for radial distortions caused by the rotation and therefore require the camera to capture images with small rotation angles. The new approach provides a significant improvement in stitching quality, especially in scenarios where the camera captures images with rotation angles greater than 60 degrees. Ultimately, our findings for the Riemann-Hilbert correspondence imply that these results on the distribution of zeros are equivalent to quantitative statements regarding the dimension growth rate of irreducible automorphic functions on $GL(n)$. This study evaluates the performance of the new edge components using reconstructed tracks from test beam data. Compared to the original design, the upgraded version demonstrates improved noise characteristics and increased hit findings along the edge. Additionally, results show that the new components can handle more intense collisions, achieving the same tracking precision of the main detector. These findings confirm the potential of the upgraded version to enhance edge reconstruction in future LHC runs. The development of full-scale upgraded forward detectors is also discussed, including proposed design variations. Finally, the performance of the pilot pilot prototypes will guide the enhancement of edge reconstruction for the CMS detector in the HL-LHC era. These resources serve as noninvertible records of the system's state and allow us to locally determine its quantum nature. Like reversible phases, quantum systems exhibit distinct periodic patterns in their tomograms, which can be used to track the unitary evolution of the system. However, the breakdown of unitary evolution leads to a distortion in the tomographic patterns, indicative of the loss of entanglement and the failure of synchronization. A specific example, the Jaynes-Cummings model, demonstrates how these tomographic patterns evolve during the transition from entanglement to decoherence and the onset of router-synchronization. The distinctive periodic patterns in the tomograms provide a clear, visual explanation for the phenomenon of cat-state formation in quantum systems. This study highlights the utility of tomographic data in the comprehensive analysis of quantum systems' behavior. Additionally, the findings suggest that tomographic patterns can serve as a more intuitive means of understanding the complex, dynamic behavior of quantum systems. The value of this approach is illustrated through its application to the Jaynes-Cummings model, which involves a two-mode system that facilitates quantum communications and has profound implications for both physics and biology. The methodology presented in this study is equally applicable to other multi-part systems that rely on quantum interactions, such as cavities with multiple inputs and output fields, quantum metrology systems, and chemical reaction networks that involve multiple entangled locations. The methods developed in this research can be used to investigate the complex dynamics of these systems, even when they are described by an unitary and nonunitary Hamiltonian that involves time-dependent parameters. The approach presented in this paper is also suitable for dealing with the interference occurring at different uncorrelated locations in these systems. Recent advances in conversational interface development focus on natural-sounding dialogues, however, ensuring understanding and proper information delivery remains a challenge. To address this issue, we propose a framework that allows for the creation of conversational interfaces with minimal programming requirements. This framework leverages large-language models, specifically models with causal language understanding capabilities, to generate responses to user input. The performance of this framework was tested with two different large-language models, Models 1 and 2, and despite Model 2's superior performance in isolated tasks, both models yielded promising results with our proposed method. Furthermore, this approach enabled the creation of a demo conversational interface with roles, showcasing both the framework's efficacy and its potential for various application scenarios. The framework's leeway for integrating additional features, such as fact-checking and more sophisticated response generation, via plugins also makes it a versatile solution. The code for this project has been made publicly available on GitHub. One key aspect of the proposed method is the use of open-source tools, both established and novel, to develop and test the conversational interface framework. These tools include Transformers like BART and ALBERT, both of which contribute to the framework's success. Additionally, both models' ability to understand and process complex, multi-part user input also plays a key role in the performance of the conversational interface. The time it takes for responses to be generated, or the latency, is another important factor but unfortunately, this aspect was not optimized in our implementation. As a result, there is a notable lag between user input and the display of conversational interface responses. This latency issue could be addressed by exploring alternative, lower-latency conversational interface development frameworks and tools. One potential shortcoming of this proposed method is the exclusive use of English language models, which may limit the applicability of this approach to other languages. However, incorporating multilingual language models into this framework could make it more language-agnostic. Another possible limitation of this method is the exclusive reliance on large-language models for understanding and processing user input and generating responses. While this approach has shown promise, integrating additional components, such as fact-checking and more sophisticated response generation via plugins, could make this method even more robust. One key advantage of this proposed method is the minimal programming requirements necessary to develop open-domain conversational interfaces. This could make it more accessible to a broader range of developers and researchers. Furthermore, this approach allows for the creation of conversational interfaces with roles, which could be especially useful in applications requiring multiple user interactions and defined roles

Tensor network representation of thermal states and temporal evolution holds significant promise for the long-term simulation of dissipative systems. However, the standard application of these methods encounters issues due to the irreversible nature of time evolution and temperature equilibrium conditions, which result from infinite-time system interactions with a heat bath. We introduce a novel, locally precise approach to describing thermal states and temporal evolution, which ensures that our representation adheres to the underlying laws of quantum mechanics, such as the principle of detailed balance, and maintains basis independence. As a result, this new method enhances the ability of tensor network simulations to accurately capture system dynamics over extended periods. We demonstrate the benefits of this approach using examples of the TN simulation technique known as univariate unrolled tensor network, which we also adapt to account for the relationship between temperature and inverse correlation lengths. Our results prove particularly useful in identifying suitable temperature ranges for this type of simulation. Furthermore, we show that the universal growth of entanglement dimensions with respect to the inverse correlation length, a crucial indicator of system size scaling, can be an unfavorable system scaling when considered in isolation. We anticipate that our new approach to time-evolved simulations will be valuable for the continued exploration of tensor network simulations. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/Thermal-TN/UTNTN. The Microscope space test for the weak equivalence principle involves measuring tiny differences in the acceleration of two test masses as they orbit the Earth. Violations of this principle would appear as periodic variations in these measurements. Specifically, a difference of $\delta a/t^2$ of $10^{-19}$ GeV/m^2 would result in an observable effect within a few months. This threat needs to be compared against regular interruptions in data, known as glitches, which can mask signal periods as short as a few seconds. This paper calculates the impact of glitches on potential periodic signals and develops a statistical method for identifying periodic variations in data sets with gaps. It was determined that with the Microscope sensor's capabilities, periodic signals as short as 10 seconds could be hidden by glitches. Furthermore, the sensitivity of this analysis has been made available for other experiments facing similar challenges. The developed algorithm can be adapted to the characteristics of specific experiments and their test masses. The Microscope team implemented measures to minimize glitches during the operation of their instrument and its successor, LUNAR. Despite this, the statistical methodology may still be relevant for such experiments. Additionally, the team is exploring the possibility of incorporating an auditory alert system into future versions of these experiments to facilitate the immediate notification of potential periodic violations of the weak equivalence principle. This could significantly shorten the time it takes to verify the results. If successful, this innovative approach could serve as a model for other gravitational physics experiments that involve searching for periodic signals in data with short timescales. The Microscope team is open to collaborating with other researchers in this field of research. Soft condensed matter systems experience significant influence from external forces,
shaping their dynamics and response to stimulation. To comprehensively study these effects,
we develop a mathematical model for the motion of particles within a gradient of activeness
that changes over time. Our analysis focuses on particles that respond actively to external
forces and the influence of their surroundings. We uncover a variety of dynamic responses,
characterized by assimilation, repulsion, or the particles moving in sync with the activeness
gradient, or even changing direction. The developed model can also be adapted to account
for particles that only react to their local environment, addressing this scenario as well.
Furthermore, our studies offer insights into the interplay between intrinsic particle properties,
their Brownian motion, and the influence of an external force field that varies spatially and
temporally. The developed model facilitates the calculation of a cross-over time, where the
particle's response shifts from following the activeness gradient to reacting to its local
environment. Additionally, we investigate how changing the strength of an external force field
can switch the particle's direction of motion. The resulting scenarios reveal complex dance
patterns, where the particle moves in a harmonic manner within the activeness gradient,
traces circular paths, or develops spiral trajectories. Our studies provide a theoretical basis
for better understanding the behavior of colloidal particles in varying activeness environments.

Furthermore, investigations reveal that the predicted behavior of the color dipole gluon distribution's mean value is consistent with lattice QCD's quark distribution's findings, and model calculations based on the JIMWLK evolution equation also align with this understanding. Additionally, research indicates that the color dipole gluon distribution's mean and variance have distinct evolution patterns. Specifically, model calculations suggest that the mean's behavior is consistent with a linear relation between the logarithm of the impact factor and the logarithm of the variable measuring x's smallness, and that the predicted impact on the proton's spin fraction is zero. On the other hand, the variance exhibits non-linear x-dependent behavior, and its study may provide insight into understanding minimum-bias event production in heavy ion collisions. Recent breakthroughs in imitation learning have significantly reduced required data for complex task mastery. However, these advances are largely confined to scenarios involving high-quality demonstrations from multiple sources. The realm of mimicry learning - which focuses on mastering a new skill by learning from a single expert demonstrator - remains underexplored and undertheorized. The process is further complicated because the demonstrator, being an expert in the target task, may not necessarily be an expert in the new environment. As a result, the demonstrator's instructions can be inaccurate or incomplete, significantly hindering the learner's progress. To address this issue, we introduce Trail, which allows the learner to tolerate some degree of error in the demonstrations, thereby enabling it to complete tasks significantly more difficult than what would be achievable with perfect guidance. By integrating both the expert's demonstrations and the learner's own experiences with the task, Trail learns a target policy by utilizing two separate networks: one for modeling the demonstrator's intentions and another for understanding the task's overall characteristics. Through extensive experiments on various benchmark tasks, we demonstrate Trail's ability to learn from subpar demonstrations, especially in scenarios involving significant environmental changes. The model's performance shows significant improvement when compared to traditional imitation learning methods, and we also provide a theoretical analysis to support our findings. With the increasing availability of crowdsourcing platforms for gathering expert data, our findings have important implications for the field of imitation learning. Current end-to-end dialogue systems rely heavily on pre-trained dialogue datasets, however these datasets are often limited in scope and poorly representative of real-world interactions due to the difficulty in gathering extensive data labeled by experts. Additionally, modern dialogue modeling often ignores the nuances of real-world conversations where multiple parties with varying levels of involvement engage in interactions. As a result, models are prone to focusing excessively on the primary speaker's messages. Our research addresses these issues by introducing a novel multi-party dialogue dataset and a new model designed to handle the complexities of real-world conversations better. This model leverages the knowledge of all participants, including the observer, to make predictions about the next dialogue message. It does this by developing a shared representation of the dialogue history from the perspective of all participants and then using this to calculate the likelihood of each possible response. We also introduce an optimized version of this model that performs equally as well but with significantly fewer parameters, thus providing a more balanced set of models suitable for evaluation purposes. Our results show that the proposed models outperform baseline multi-agent expert-annotated models and that the optimized model achieves comparable performance to the standard model but with improved generalizability. As might be expected, the greatest improvements in performance are realized when the co-observer's turns contain more informative messages. We examine the property of having a finite word problem for the R. Thompson group V, considering various related problems about V's combinatorial structure. Some of the studied questions remain unresolved, and we provide partial results for specific combinatorial questions regarding V's hierarchy of subgroups, its intersection with group combinatorial dynamics, and the properties of nearly surjective elements within V. Our research also explores the relationship between V's word problem and its distinguished subgroups, particularly identifying the type of the word problem for V's hierarchy of subgroups, as well as determining the complexity of nearly surjective elements within V and their intersection with the Baer-Schreier theorem. Finally, we discuss the connection between V's word problem and its combinatorial structure, including V's hierarchy of subgroups, nearly surjective elements, and the Baer-Schreier theorem, establishing a fundamental link between these aspects of V's structure. This establishes a kind of 'efficient' aspect of V's combinatorial structure, despite V being a group with a complex, intricate nature. This work is the outcome of a research collaboration with Thomas Koberda and Daniel T. Thomas. We have made the computations and findings publicly available for reproducibility and further exploration. Additionally, we have addressed an open problem related to group dynamics, specifically asking about the fate of the word problem for group doubles under the Baer-Schreier extension, solving a related problem about the type of the word problem for group doubles, and even generalizing this result to a broader category of groups. This solution, in turn, has implications for the type of the word problem for V's hierarchy of subgroups and nearly surjective elements within V. This work not only advances our understanding of the intricate R. Thompson group V but also contributes to a more comprehensive theory of group combinatorics. This research focuses on the steady-state behavior of a periodically driven and coupled quantum system, specifically two qubits in the shape of a X, which experiences periodic driving forces. The study reveals that in a regime far from equilibrium, a steady-state state of perfect entanglement can be achieved when the system is subjected to periodic driving, even when working with a heat bath. The research also finds that this result isn't limited to entanglement, as any mixed-state component can also be perfected. MongoDB is a widely used, document-oriented, NoSQL database that is increasingly part of critical information systems. Given the high-risk nature of these systems, ensuring transactional integrity is a significant concern, yet there is a lack of effective methods for validating the transactional property known as "partial integrity." This property ensures that a database schedule does not violate any constraint until the end of the transaction. To address this gap, we have developed a practical approach for validating the transactional property of partial integrity in MongoDB. Our method is efficient, as it determines whether a database schedule violates a constraint in constant time. This efficiency allows our approach to validate the integrity of MongoDB schedules in a real-world scenario, as demonstrated by our experiments using the YCSB and Amazon Dynamo workloads. Furthermore, our method can be applied to other key-value stores that support atomic put operations. The source code of this tool is available for other researchers to use. Current advancements in medical image analysis are hindered by cultural and racial biases embedded in image collections and annotation practices.  Despite the seemingly neutral intentions of practitioners, these biases persist and are reflected in datasets such as MIOFER, specifically in annotations regarding disease presence/absence.  A potential source of these biases lies in the algorithms used for preprocessing segments of anatomical interest (SAMs).  Used extensively in the medical imaging field, popular SAMs extraction algorithms like SIFT and SUPERASIFT have inherent biases rooted in their design.  To illustrate this issue, this paper puts the widely-used SIFT algorithm under scrutiny.  By manipulating SIFT parameters such as contrast and scale, this paper demonstrates how it exhibits a form of intrinsic bias known as "binarity".  To mitigate such biases in medical image analysis tasks, this paper proposes the use of alternative algorithms like RIFT which outperforms SIFT and SUPERASIFT in multiple benchmark datasets.  To support this argument, this paper includes results from an evaluation of RIFT, SIFT, and SUPERASIFT on multiple medical image classification and detection tasks using various datasets such as MIOFER, Vertebral Artery Variations, and Vertebral Artery Occlusion.  Furthermore, this paper is also available as a part of the recent BiAS workshop at the IEEE CVPR 2021 conference.  Code for this project is available at https://github.com/andersonbreton/InnateBiasDetection.  The reason for releasing this work previously at the BiAS workshop was to facilitate the exchange of ideas among researchers in the medical image analysis community to address the critical issue of algorithmic bias. We present the findings of a nuclear forward scattering study on the Bi$_5$FeTi$_3$O$_{15}$ (BFTO) quadruple layered Aurivillius compound as pressure is increased in an attempt to locate a reported high-pressure magnetic ground state.  Our data, collected to 45 GPa, reveal that the BFTO anti-ferromagnetic order present at ambient conditions persists up to 10 GPa, where we also find structural changes which result in the expansion of TiO$_8$ boxes.  Beyond this point, we observe the magnetic order changes to ferromagnetic, yet this shift is not accompanied by the anticipated electric conductivity change or the expansion of the TiO$_8$ box in a manner consistent with increased size.  Conversely, the structural modification reverts back to that seen at ambient pressure above 30 GPa, where we also note the re-emergence of the anti-ferromagnetic order.  We propose an electronic configuration involving Ti $3d$ bands to explain these outcomes, where the pressure-driven movement of these bands results in changes to spin alignment.  We hope the insights gained from these measurements will guide theoretical predictions and further studies on this and related materials.  We also note that even though we were unable to verify the reported ferromagnetic state at high pressure with our more sensitive nuclear forward scattering measurements, our study still offers a different perspective on the magnetic and structural properties of BFTO under pressure.  We conclude by suggesting that further research is warranted to fully comprehend the magnetic and structural properties of BFTO and other related materials under the influence of increased pressure. Researchers typically model the mean density of the current cosmic matter distribution using an average density, $\rho_m$, and assume a given average temperature, $T_0$. However, the actual density varies significantly, following a power law similar to $\rho \propto s^{-n}$, where $s$ represents the ratio of a specific distance to the current mean distance. The density at any given distance can be converted into a probability distribution of overdensities, $\delta$, relative to the average density. We analyze the fundamental limitations of measuring phase dynamics in planar superconducting devices, specifically junctions and SQUIDs, due to their inherent area uncertainty, unitarity, and temperature-based decay. Our investigation reveals the suitability of two figures of merit, the phase relaxation time and effective area, for characterizing these devices' phase dynamics. Based on these quantities, we provide guidelines for designing devices that meet specific application requirements, including those necessary for quantum simulations, stochastic quantum computing, and certain universal operations. Additionally, we discuss the relevance of these principles to other devices that involve phase degrees of freedom. Furthermore, we propose a figure of merit, known as the critical current uncertainty, that characterizes the switching current of these devices and provides insights into their phase dynamics. Building on previous work, we introduce an alternative method for determining the phase relaxation time and effective area from switching current measurements. We also explore the relationship between switching current measurements and phase dynamics in the context of quantum simulations, highlighting the potential for both agreement and discrepancy. Lastly, we discuss various strategies for optimizing the phase relaxation time and effective area through material modifications, design adjustments, and control of the measurement environment. We examine the utility of our framework for evaluating the suitability of devices for quantum applications through a detailed analysis of a specific example. Additionally, we discuss the complementary nature of switching current and interference-based measurements, discussing potential improvements to our framework and the broader scope of devices involving phase degrees of freedom. Lastly, we outline potential research directions for further investigation.

Given a subset $A$ of the $\ell_p$ space and an $\varepsilon>0$, we define an $\varepsilon$-isometric linear dimension decrease for $A$ as the smallest number $\text{isd}_\varepsilon(A)$ such that there exists a $p$-Schatten operator $T$ on a Hilbert space $H$, a unitary operator $U$ on the subspace spanned by $A$, and a subspace $B$ of $H$ such that: (1) $\|Tx\|_p \approx \varepsilon\|x\|_p$ for all $x\in A$, (2) $\text{dim}_p(B) \leq (1+\varepsilon)^2 \text{dim}_p(A)$, and (1+\varepsilon)^{-1}\|x\|_p \leq \|Ux\|_p \leq (1+\varepsilon)\|x\|_p for all $x\in B$, implying that we have an isometric linear dimension decrease of order $\varepsilon$ on $A$. We prove that $\text{isd}_\varepsilon(A) \leq (1+\varepsilon)^{2d-1}$ when $A$ is an $(d-1)$-dimensional unit ball in the $\ell_p$ space, and we also show that this inequality is optimal when $d=1$. Additionally, we extend the $\varepsilon$-isometric linear dimension decrease property to incompressible subsets of the $\ell_p$ space, and we establish a connection with the Schur property of operator spaces. Finally, we investigate the $\varepsilon$-isometric linear dimension decrease of unit balls in the $\ell_p$ space with $p<1$, and we discuss the related issue of finding the smallest $p$-Schatten norm of a subunitary operator on a Hilbert space. The study of instrumental systematic errors during Cosmic Microwave Background (CMB) experiments is complex due to the extensive customization of instruments for each experiment, often featuring custom designs and techniques. This specialization makes it difficult for researchers to rely on existing resources and tools, such as data analysis software and models of instrumental performance, which are often tailored to other experiments and are therefore ineffective. This paper presents an open-source Python package named s4cmb, which provides a unified framework for modeling the performance of CMB experiments, including their spectral characteristics, beam patterns, and map simulations from sky simulations. This framework can be extended to accommodate various experimental configurations through its modular design, featuring customizable models of instrumental systematic errors and simulation of affected maps through a degrading process. This approach can be used to evaluate the effectiveness of experimental design parameters, such as beam shapes and sizes, through the simulation of instrumental systematic errors. The paper showcases the capabilities of s4cmb using data from the BOLDO experiment, an ground-based CMB experiment that studied the Galactic Center. In recent years, pre-trained language models have achieved remarkable success in various natural language processing tasks. Despite this success, research into the internal workings of these models remains limited. This study dives deeper into the performance of pre-trained language models on a fundamental task - arranging words in a meaningful order. We utilize BART as a case study and discover that its word arrangement capability relies on a complex interplay between multiple aspects, including order-specific preferences, syntactic patterns, and semantic coherence. Our analysis showcases that while BART excels at capturing general language properties, its limited scope can also lead to arranges that, while syntactically sound, lack semantic sense. We conclude that word arrangement is more than just a straightforward summarization task and that pre-trained language models bring a range of biases to the table. The rapid dissemination of ultra-realistic media content, particularly videos, has exacerbated the issue of deepfake propaganda. Analyzing an entire video using this approach, however, proves computationally expensive and impractical for current applications. This paper introduces a pioneering methodology for identifying deepfakes in video frames, building upon the success of earlier non-video approaches. Initially, a cross-sequence attention mechanism is proposed to capture a video's temporal characteristics. This concept is then expanded upon to create a novel, multi-domain cross-sequence attention framework that can be applied to detect deepfakes from audio and video feeds. This model is referred to as the MD-CSDNetwork. Implementing this model as a part of a comprehensive evaluation framework, we conduct numerous experiments with various attention-based prototypes and find that our proposed MD-CSDNetwork method achieves superior performance on multiple deepfake datasets. Furthermore, we demonstrate the efficacy of our approach by applying it to detect manipulation in real-world video clips. The study of low-density parity-check (LDPC) codes has been a significant area of research in recent years. However, a crucial aspect that has been overlooked is the degree distribution of the LDPC ensemble, specifically its impact on the performance of the decoder when operating on a binary erasure channel. In an effort to address this gap, our research examines various degree distributions in relation to their decoding outcomes and identifies several patterns. We demonstrate that two newly proposed degree distributions, 'alternating' and 'adjacent', consistently yield superior decoding results when compared to the standard 'uniform' degree distribution. These findings have the potential to guide the design of LDPC codes with optimized performance. We also introduce a new metric called the 'degree-related correlation' and show that it is a key factor in predicting the outcome of the decoder. Building upon this understanding, we are able to create a more efficient decoding algorithm, 'adjacent' degree-driven, which outperforms the conventional Gallager-A (GA) decoder. The adjacent degree-driven decoder is a key innovation in our research, allowing us to probe the limits of LDPC codes on a binary erasure channel. We are able to use this new decoder to design LDPC codes with extremely high information rates, significantly higher than what is currently achievable with GA decoding. For example, our research enables the creation of LDPC codes with information rates up to 0.95, a rate that cannot be achieved with GA decoding. We are also able to demonstrate that two other degree distributions, 'double' and 'triple', yield superior decoding results when the number of variable nodes is an even or odd number respectively. Furthermore, our research shows that the best degree distribution is dependent on the number of variable nodes, a finding with important implications for the design of LDPC codes. Building upon these insights, we are able to design a new class of LDPC codes, called degree-degree related low-density parity-check (DDR-LDPC) codes, which store memory information about the degree of each node. We are able to use this new storage capability to further enhance the performance of the decoder, a technique that can also be applied to other types of codes. The resulting DDR-LDPC codes outperform conventional LDPC codes by a significant margin, as evidenced by the results presented in our thesis. We have discovered that an eavesdropper can easily bypass the system's security function by utilizing a simple technique known as hacking. This technique exploits the randomness of the system's phase to create various possible attacks, which can result in an average attack rate that is significantly higher than expected, potentially up to 50.25% in the case of the four-phase-state protocol. This rate increase presents a significant obstacle to the practical implementation of quantum key distribution systems. We have also found that the security of these systems can be restored by introducing random phase changes among source states, which prevents an eavesdropper from controlling the system and selecting the most advantageous attacks. The new approach to quantum key distribution, utilizing a combination of random polarization and phase, offers improved protection against hacking and can result in much higher secure average rates of around 50.25% in the case of the four-phase-state protocol. The effectiveness of this restoration method is verified through real-world demonstrations of both unprotected and protected versions of the quantum key distribution system. The former example, which failed to meet the minimum required security standard, was able to generate around 1.67 x 10^11 bits in just 1 second of operation, while the protected version, which met the security standard, was able to generate approximately 2.26 x 10^11 secure bits in the same time frame. The restoration method, however, came with a cost, as the addition of the phase randomization component reduced the average secure rate by a small amount, to around 49.75%. The impact of this reduction is considered acceptable, given the significant increase in security it provides. The new approach to quantum key distribution is therefore both efficient and secure. This technique can be applied to a wide range of quantum state protocols, including both binary and multi-level protocols, and is particularly effective against systems based on the measurement of momentum, which is the most commonly used configuration. In 1930, K. Menger developed the concept of an angle function, which can be applied to the metric space to obtain a measure for angles between vectors. However, Menger identified limitations to this development by stating that the introduced angle function may not satisfy the basic properties of angle measurements, specifically those of Minkowski. Despite initial interest from researchers such as J. von Neumann, the concept of angle spaces did not gain significant traction and eventually faded from mathematical reference. This paper revisits the ideas of Menger on angle spaces and offers a groundbreaking solution to two unresolved problems posed by Menger in his original works. The first problem concerned finding the smallest possible dimension for angle spaces, while the second involved determining whether the space of angle functions is homeomorphic to a Euclidean space. This research builds upon earlier findings and provides a more comprehensive understanding of the underlying theory. The novel solution to the second problem involves a topological invariant and reveals that the space of angle functions has a structure analogous to a Euclidean space in dimensions two and higher, while in dimension one it exhibits a more complex relationship with Euclidean spaces. Additionally, this research can be applied to a broader category of metric spaces, as well as certain spaces defined by angle measurements. While angular momentum conservation would lead to rapidly spinning and thinning disks, the release of angular momentum through viscous forces slows their spin. This process also creates spiral density waves that can amplify the disk's surface density, potentially leading to increased solid particle delivery to planetary accretion sites. Despite its importance, the mechanism of viscous disk evolution remains poorly understood, particularly in its early stages. Recent studies have shed new light on this process, particularly in regards to the development of whirlpools in disks, which could significantly impact the distribution of solid particles. This integrated approach could provide a more comprehensive understanding of the processes that shape protoplanetary disks and give rise to planetary systems. We introduce a novel character map called cluster character for the representation theory of quantum groups, specifically those associated with simply-laced types. This character map applies to irreducible modules and their highest weight counterparts, and interestingly, it relates to the Fock-Goncharov duality framework. A key feature of the cluster character is its explicit computation via an invariant value, tied to the non-degenerate grid within the corresponding Poisson variety. A further notable aspect is that the sum of the cluster characters for all irreducible modules equivalent to a given highest weight module is equivalent to that highest weight module itself. Moreover, we demonstrate that the cluster character of a module is an algebraic variant of the Fock-Goncharov character, and that this connection holds even in cases where the character does not separate modules. Building on this foundation, we explore further results, including a realization of the cluster character as a mixture of the Fock-Goncharov and Lusztig characters, as well as an identification of the Euler product in our setting with the product of refined cluster characters. Ultimately, our findings establish a direct link between the representation theory of quantum groups and the grid-based algebras underlying the realm of cluster algebras, revealing a richer structure within the quantum group representations. The development of hard-drive storage technology was instrumental in accelerating the processing speed of computers, allowing for numerous advancements in science, engineering, and economics. Through the lens of computer architecture, this lecture series for advanced undergraduate and graduate students explores the transformation of computers from slow, tape-driven machines to fast, internally stored computers. We examine the computational challenges of the past, the development of computer architectures in response to these challenges, and the impact of programming methodologies on both computers and problems being solved. A key focus is on the role of storage systems in computer architecture, with an in-depth examination of the transition from slow tape drives to fast internal disks. Finally, the lecture series concludes by considering the current and future implications of storage systems on computer architecture, including the rising importance of memory hierarchy once again.  As part of this exploration, the series delves into three notable computational problems - numerical integration, molecular dynamics, and gravitational n-body problems - to demonstrate the emergence of hard drives as the dominant computer storage technology and the resulting memory hierarchy, which will continue to shape computer design in the future. Pyramid scams, a centuries-old investment deception, rely on high-ranking participants who profit from new recruits in a hierarchical network of defrauded members. The introduction of blockchain technology and smart contracts has generated significant interest in decentralized applications, but the underlying structure of pyramid schemes remains poorly understood. This research unveils the intricate mechanisms of a sophisticated pyramid scheme built with smart contracts, known as Forsage, by dissecting its cryptographic underpinnings, user interaction protocols, and the pseudorandom distribution of bonuses. By analyzing transaction data from the Binance Smart Chain, we have identified the scheme's enslaving potential, the limited benefits for the majority of participants, and the concentration of wealth among the top-tier scammers. Furthermore, we have found that the scheme's promises of limitless potential for participants are misleading, and the promises of high returns for the leaders are false, with no genuine incentive for referral, as the bonus paid to lower-level participants is deducted from the sale of new contracts by the seller. The sale of Forsage contracts is deemed unfair business practices and the company behind it is being sued in the United States. The scheme has also been reported to the Federal Trade Commission (FTC) and the SEC in the United States, SEPA in Europe and the Australian Securities and Investments Commission (ASIC). The code and data used in this study are available for download at https://github.com/andersonzelho/forsage. The analysis of this pyramid scheme may offer valuable insights for researchers studying the underlying structure of other cryptocurrency schemes, such as Ponzi and pyramid schemes, cryptocurrency scams and fraudulent initial coin offerings (ICOs). The Forsage code provides an interesting case study for the analysis of smart contract-based schemes, such as those built with Solana, Elrond and EOS, among others. The data used in this study may also be used in conjunction with other datasets to create more comprehensive graphs and a deeper understanding of the blockchain architecture of these types of schemes. We investigated 19 potential globular clusters within the Milky Way's bulge using infrared images from the VVV survey. Our analysis involved precise position calculations and subsequent comparisons with previous findings. While we confirmed the general locations of the proposed clusters, we were unable to verify the suggested radii in most cases. Further research into these candidates is essential to fully determine their characteristics and distinguish them from the numerous compact star collections within the bulge. Our initial exploration included the assessment of general population demographics within the proposed clusters, along with assessments of their radial profiles, density distributions, and color-magnitude patterns. Our research reveals that a particular sub-class of these networks, characterized by 'hyper-invariant' symmetry, are remarkably efficient in achieving this goal, even when dealing with systems that have more complex, exponential correlation structures, rather than power-law correlations.  Our findings demonstrate that hyper-invariant MERA circuits can exhibit behavior akin to quantum systems that utilize area-law entanglement patterns, such as quantum anti-ferromagnetic systems, but now also encompass systems that exhibit exponential decay of correlations, such as certain classes of rotators and interactive circulant systems, all from a fundamental perspective of the network's architecture.  We also introduce a simpler 'weak' variant of these circuits, which also accurately represent systems with power-law correlations and also possesses architectural similarities to the standard MERA circuit, albeit without the complex 'unsmoothed' part.
