Microblogging platforms like Twitter offer valuable insights into disaster relief efforts and public opinion, which can be obtained through social mirror APIs but are no longer available due to licensing costs and data privacy concerns. Alternatively, firehose access can be acquired from the platform directly, which however requires meeting specific criteria including the fulfillment of data retention policies set by the region in question. Given that Twitter data storage is limited to 7 days in Turkey, obtaining suitable datasets for analysis becomes even more difficult. This research seeks to illustrate the difficulties encountered when analyzing Twitter data related to the Izmir earthquake, which occurred in October 2020, due to these data retention constraints. It is worth noting that the used dataset was stored in the University of Marmara's database, to which access was granted following the fulfillment of certain criteria. Nonetheless, even with access granted, there were still limitations imposed by the 7-day data storage period in Turkey, which significantly hindered the analysis. In the case study presented, only the initial responses to the earthquake, which occurred 6 days prior to the data collection, could be analyzed. It is also worth noting that a methodological framework was proposed alongside the Izmir earthquake case study, which serves as an essential starting point for any scholar seeking to conduct similar research. This proposed framework addresses numerous challenges, which are discussed in the form of Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs). It is our hope that this proposed framework will contribute positively to the advancement of Twitter data analysis in Turkey and facilitate the answer to at least one of the many questions still pending in this field. This paper is an extension of an earlier study presented at the 7th International Conference on Advanced Research in Virtual and Physical Learning Environments (AIVILEL 2021). It is also a follow-up to the paper titled "Examination of Twitter Data in Turkey" (AIVILEL 2021). This later edition of that paper is now available in the Proceedings of the 8th International Conference on Advanced Research in Virtual and Physical Learning Environments (AIVILEL 2022). It is also our hope that this later edition of that paper will be of greater use to all scholars working with Twitter data in Turkey. It is our hope that both the earlier and the later editions of this paper will be of use to Dr. Rahayu, who passed away in 2021 and to whom this paper is dedicated in remembrance. A massive stellar explosion in AD Leo occurred on April 12, 1985, where the star suddenly increased in brightness by a thousandfold in the near-ultraviolet range.  Researchers studied the interaction between the hot star and its surrounding circumstellar material, using computational modeling to examine the evolving spectrum from the explosion.  By modeling the expanding shock wave and the decreasing temperature of the front edge, researchers simulated the spectrum at different stages of the explosion's evolution, using 5000K to 18,000K temperatures and analyzing the spectra at 13 days, 57 days, and 114 days after the event.  A good match was found between the modeled and actual spectra of the star at these time periods.  Modeling also indicated that any pre-existing accretion layers on AD Leo would likely be too thin to cause significant variation in its brightness in the ultraviolet range.  Furthermore, the relatively slow decline in the ultraviolet light curve of AD Leo might be attributed to additional external shocks produced by the interaction between the expanding front edge and any nearby companion star, although this hypothesis needs further observation to be confirmed.  Using the AD Leo data as examples, the general principles of analyzing great outbursts in magnetic binary systems are discussed.  The distinction is drawn between two types of explosions: (1) those associated with an expanding shock wave, as seen in AD Leo, and (2) those characterized by the instantaneous disappearance of the white dwarf's light, as seen in the 1975 eruption of U Geminorum, where the permanent dimming indicates mass transfer from the accretion disk to the white dwarf.  Theoretical computer simulations of the 1985 outburst of AD Leo are the basis for a new one-zone model for the star's UV spectrum, and this model is made publicly available.  This new approach, however, only applies to binary systems with a low-mass accretion disk, as in the case of AD Leo, and not to systems with a high accretion rate throughout the disk, as discussed in a related paper. We find that the network's structure affects the mode of the field's mode expansion, and this in turn influences the effective action's expansion in the form of a beta function. The effective action is examined in detail for several specific network configurations, including a fully connected graph and a graph representing a fractional quantum Hall system. The behavior of the effective action's modes is found to either converge to a fixed point, diverge due to a barrier, or converge to a plateau point. The critical temperature that separates these regimes is indicated by an equilibrium scale that contrasts with the typical scale of the network's correlation length. This research introduces a novel smoothing algorithm called TPC, designed to maintain the intrinsic geometry of a 3D point cloud by eliminating non-manifold edges. TPC achieves this by creating a dual surface mesh, smoothing this surface using Lapalce-Beltrami-Weingarten (LBW) method, and then mapping the smoothed surface back to the original point cloud. We demonstrate TPC's effectiveness in preserving the unique structure of a 3D model by comparing its results to other smoothing techniques. Additionally, we apply TPC to a real-world task, specifically removing snow from a 3D city map, and show that its ability to preserve the model's underlying structure is crucial for accurate output. We make TPC available as an open-source implementation in Python. 

However, our implementation has several limitations and relies on precomputed information about a 3D model's topology, which can be difficult to obtain accurately. To address these challenges, we propose an alternative approach called PCC, a Python-based 3D processing framework that incorporates TPC and other smoothening techniques. We also explore a possibility of integrating PCC with the MeshLab software. 

Despite its promising results, our study has several restrictions. Firstly, the evaluation of TPC's performance is limited to visual assessments alone. Secondly, the removal of snow from a 3D city map is carried out manually, which is not a fully automated process. Lastly, the computational cost of the LBW method is higher than other smoothing techniques, which could present issues for complex 3D models. Lastly, the smoothing of non-manifold edges in a 3D point cloud is currently only achievable up to a triangulated surface. Therefore, future research could focus on enhancing the performance of the LBW method, exploring more efficient smoothing techniques, and developing a fully automated approach to removing snow from a 3D city map.

Temporal knowledge graph completion has emerged as a leading approach for inferring accurate and missing event and temporal knowledge graph information. Unlike traditional static knowledge graph completion, this task deals with temporal relationships and events with clear timelines. A key challenge here is modeling temporal relations and capturing information that varies over time. Former approaches primarily employed time-aware encoding strategies for temporal relations and event-based representation learning, but they often failed to capture global low-rarity information and the high-ranking complexity of graphs. In this paper, we introduce a novel framework known as T-KG2Vec, which utilizes a graph attention network to learn event representations and then applies a low-rank matrix factorization technique to the resulting representation. This dual-approach not only enhances the efficacy of models but also offers an extra layer of flexibility in the dimensionality of representations. We evaluate the performance of T-KG2Vec on three temporal knowledge graph datasets, and the results demonstrate its superiority over existing state-of-the-art models. The source code of the model is available at https://github.com/hkz2018/T-KG2Vec. The model also outperformed state-of-the-art approaches in the recent Paper Abstracts at the 2021 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing, earning them 6th and 7th place respectively. We have also conducted thorough experiments using the publicly available datasets available at https://github.com/hkz2018/T-KG2Vec-Extra. We have further validated the interpretability of the representations learned with T-KG2Vec by analyzing the embedding of temporal relations, event roles, and entities. The embeddings of all entities and events are made available at https://github.com/hkz2018/T-KG2Vec-Extra. The model has the advantage of model-neutral temporal relation representations, offering immense potential for further exploration in the domain. We have explored this possibility by employing the representations learned from T-KG2Vec as input to additional models, including convolutional neural networks, graph neural networks, and matrix factorization. The model outperformed all baselines in our experiments, and we have provided a detailed comparison of our approach with existing techniques. The novel low-rank constraint on representation learning, the unique application of graph attention networks to time-aware event representation learning, and the innovative use of temporal relation information have all been documented in our in-depth analysis. We have also demonstrated the efficacy of our approach by conducting extensive experiments. Utilizing an exact RPA eigenvector solver, a detailed investigation was conducted to explore the complex nature of RPA eigenvalues within the GDR spectrum of $^{16}$O. The study revealed that both the real and imaginary components of the RPA eigenenergies contribute to the width and shape of the photoresponse cross-section. The idea that life could be transferred from one planetary system to another, a concept known as interstellar panspermia, has its roots in the distant past, but the challenge remains of identifying evidence to support this theory. To address this issue, researchers have developed statistical models to determine the likelihood of asteroid and comet deliveries from other star systems, involving intricate astrobiological, astronomical, and mathematical components. This work delves into a crucial aspect of those models, specifically the probability of viable organisms reaching other planets on cometary asteroids, a phenomenon known as the "delivery efficiency." A critical factor in this context is the "viability time," which is defined as the duration an organism can survive while traveling through interstellar space. This paper examines how viability time interacts with delivery efficiency and determines the most restrictive condition, also known as the "viability constraint," which includes aspects like the reach of our cosmic neighborhood and the capabilities of Earth's microbial resistance. A key finding is that all discovered Earth organisms can withstand for approximately 10 to 100 million years; however, this survival period is significantly shorter for any potential extraterrestrial life, narrowing the viable distance to 100 parsecs over the next 10 million years. This constraint also limits delivery opportunities to only a small percentage of nearby asteroid and comet arrivals, resulting in a much lower probability of detecting interstellar panspermia, a risk that could be as rare as 0.01 percent or less. Nevertheless, this discovery does not dismiss the possibility of interstellar panspermia, as there are numerous aspects still to be explored, along with potential avenues for scientists to further refine the viability time and delivery efficiency, ultimately leading to a more precise understanding of this complex issue. This work underscores the significance of considering viability time and viability time distributions when evaluating the possibility of interstellar panspermia, a topic that continues to be a subject of interest for both scientific and philosophical communities. As research unfolds, there is the potential for statisticians and astrobiologists to collaborate more closely, with a corresponding increase in the need for validity checks, a broader examination of viability time, and a more detailed analysis of the viability constraint, leading to a clearer understanding of this captivating phenomenon. As the search for extraterrestrial life accelerates through missions like TESS and ARROW, a deeper understanding of the viability time and viability constraint will be crucial in appropriately interpreting potential discoveries, as the possibility of confirming interstellar panspermia remains a promising outcome, though likely to be a rare event. Unlike traditional methods that rely on tailored algorithms for specific formats, our uniform sampling strategy is a more adaptable and general solution for a wider range of visual templates. Network polarization refers to the limited exchange of influence or information within isolated, highly connected components of a network, contrasted with the diversified, extensive connections across a broader network scope. Accurate measurements of polarization rely on methods that distinguish this phenomenon from network disturbances, such as the formation of closed groups based on opposing views. A fundamental task in a distributed network is estimating the size of the graph. This task becomes even more complex when the network contains a large artificial world within it, consisting of multiple heavily interconnected components. The existing approaches to estimate the graph size are vulnerable to manipulation by an adversary that can create and control a significant number of false nodes. We have developed a new method to estimate the graph size in the presence of a large artificial world within the network and a limited number of malicious nodes. This estimation algorithm requires a time of O(D) and a memory of O(1) among a total of O(N) nodes in the network, where N represents the actual size of the network, D denotes the depth of the artificial world, and C is the cluster number indicating the number of large components in the network. Notably, both the time and memory requirements of our estimator are independent of the size of the individual components within the artificial world. Moreover, our approach is optimal in the sense that in a specific scenario with only two components, the space and time requirements can be shown to be optimal under certain conditions. A novel component detection algorithm is also presented, which may be of independent interest. This algorithm can detect two large components within an unweighted graph by exchanging only O(log* N) bits of information between nodes. A broader framework for the design of robust distributed algorithms under the influence of an adversary is also discussed. This framework can be applied to create a range minimum query solution that is resilient to a large artificial world within the network. Finally, both the graph size estimation and the component detection algorithms can be extended to a variety of other applications. This selected set of patterns becomes the basis for estimating future traffic conditions. To evaluate our approach, we used real-world traffic data from San Francisco and New York City, simulating the performance of our method with random subset selections as a benchmark. Our results showed that our technique consistently produced more accurate predictions than the baseline method. Furthermore, we applied our method to a practical problem, developing an algorithm to identify optimal time windows for visitors to arrive at Stanford University's Serra Mall. Our findings highlighted the importance of considering recent traffic conditions along with longer-term patterns. This combination of recent and historical data led to more effective queue size predictions and, by extension, more accurate arrival time recommendations for visitors. In simulations of complex astrophysical phenomena involving compact objects, where matter is influenced by gravity and other interactions, resolving the earliest stages of the process poses significant constraints on numerical relativity simulations. Our proposed method, known as Conformal Transverse-Traceless deformation of the background metric, addresses these limitations by bypassing the need for initial data that satisfies the constraints, thus allowing for the introduction of distortions from a given background metric. This approach leverages the existence of long-wavelength modes in field equations and enables a deformation of the initial data while still adhering to the Einstein field equations. By defining a suitable Hamiltonian that encompasses the deformation, we demonstrate that this approach preserves the first law of mechanics for the compact objects' masses and linear and angular momenta. Our technique, called CTTK, specifically facilitates the introduction of perturbations in compact objects' interiors by deforming their geometry rather than their Weyl scalar, thus allowing for a broader range of studies in numerical relativity with improved accuracy and stability. We showcase CTTK's capabilities in multiple simulations, including binary black hole mergers and the collapse of massive stars leading to a binary system of black holes and a perturbed start of black hole formation from a collapsed matter cloud. Our research highlights the advantages of CTTK over other constraint-satisfying approaches in numerical relativity. By bypassing the constraints, CTTK enhances the accuracy of simulations while reducing the computational costs and alleviating the stringent requirements on initial data. This technique is particularly beneficial for analyzing the behavior of quasars and supercritical collapse in dust-filled spaces, such as in binary neutron star mergers. Our findings also indicate that the overproduction of gravitational waves reported in initial data-driven simulations may be attributed to the violation of the Einstein equations rather than any flaw in the code. Consequently, this discovery may lead to a major redevelopment of existing numerical relativity codes to incorporate the improved algorithms presented in this research. Additionally, our research demonstrates that the information contained in the long-wavelength modes of the Hamiltonian can be extracted after the deformation, which potentially enables a more straightforward reconstruction of the initial data. This, in turn, may enable the reverse engineering of complex processes, such as quasars, to gain a deeper understanding of the underlying physics. Furthermore, this technique may also facilitate a more direct link between numerical relativity simulations and analytical solutions, such as those derived from perturbation theory. Our research provides novel insights into the behavior of compact objects and the complex astrophysical processes involving them

Pieter Johannes van Rhijn took over as director of Kapteyn's Astronomical Observatory in 1911 and effectively carried out Jacobus Kapteyn's "Star Stream" vision until his death in 1945.  Upon assuming the role, van Rhijn prioritized the completion of Kapteyn's plan and assembled a team to execute the tasks.  Together they finished the "Catalogus van de 6000 sterksten Sterren in het Zonnetoegang" and began observing variable stars to support Henry Draper's research.  Notably, van Rhijn also established the New General Catalogue in collaboration with Jan Hendrik Oort.  During his tenure as director, van Rhijn made significant contributions, including developing the "Scheme of Selected Areas" to further explore the Star Stream concept.  This plan involved in-depth studies of 31 regions near the Sun and was carried out with the use of the wide-field telescope and photometric instruments van Rhijn designed and constructed with the assistance of the Dutch optical manufacturer, Utrecht's Joh. Hartmann & Sohn.  The "Scheme of Selected Areas" aimed to investigate the Sun's neighborhood and identify relationships among stars in the foreground and background.  The photometric methods developed during this project allowed van Rhijn to determine the luminosity of numerous stars and ultimately paved the way for his later work as secretary general of the International Astronomical Union.  This work also laid the groundwork for the research of later generations of astronomers.  Throughout his life, van Rhijn was driven by a passion for astronomy and a desire to contribute to the field's advancement, leaving a lasting legacy in the development of the study of our solar neighborhood.  This biography of van Rhijn is a compilation of previously published information and personal recollections from his time at the Kapteyn Astronomical Observatory as both director and employee, offering an in-depth look at his life and the significant impact he had on the development of astronomy.  Van Rhijn passed away on July 17, 1973, at the age of 86, leaving behind his wife, Anna, who he married in 1920 and had two children with. Since the discovery of the major elements, numerous compounds have been characterized through physical and chemical properties, leading to an understanding of the periodic table's underlying structure. However, despite this knowledge, many properties of elements and their compounds remain unexplained. Recent studies suggest that this lack of explanation might be attributed to a long-forgotten theory proposed in the 19th century by the chemist and philosopher John Herschel, who hypothesized that the diversity of compounds could be explained by the inherent 'cleverness' or reactivity of elements. We examine Herschel's idea within the framework of modern chemistry and physics, and propose a quantitative measure of an element's 'cleverness' that is based on its ability to form stable compounds and contribute to their stability. By applying this approach to all naturally occurring elements and their compounds, we found a positive correlation between the average 'cleverness' of elements and the number of possible compounds, and uncovered 'cleverness' patterns within the periodic table. Moreover, we identified a group of elements that, according to our measure, are not very 'clever' but manage to form a substantial number of stable compounds by also being quite'sensible' (stable) and tend to avoid reactions with other elements. We also discovered a few 'clever' elements that not only readily form compounds but also tend to do so unstable compounds and we propose that the latter might be responsible for the abundance of heavy elements in the universe. Finally, we discuss the implication of our research on the field of astrochemistry and the formation of heavy elements in stars and planets.

We have designed a novel control framework that can learn optimal control policies from minimal, irrelevant, and possibly fake data. This framework can be applied to a wide range of complex dynamic systems and can handle excessive or irrelevant side information. We demonstrated the effectiveness of this framework by applying it to three challenging systems: a highly responsive aerodynamic vehicle, a brain-based walking robot, and an underwater robot. The only side information available for these systems was their state-space diagrams, dynamic equations, and detailed descriptive articles. We compared our framework's performance to traditional methods that require extensive, relevant data and found it produced comparable results with more than 100 times less training data. This framework can also learn controllable states, refine existing policies, and successfully transfer policies to similar systems. Notably, we successfully trained an underwater robot controller using data from a flying robot, even though the two systems have fundamentally different dynamics. This breakthrough could significantly accelerate the development of complex autonomous systems by enabling the use of existing models for quick, data-driven optimization. This new approach could particularly benefit systems with many controllable states, making it a significant advancement in autonomous development. This study seeks to offer a distanced yet precise method for examining the impact of remote learning on student persistence in higher education during the COVID-19 pandemic. We demonstrate that Coxeter groups possess biautomatic properties, resulting from which we derive that uniform lattices within isometry groups of buildings also exhibit biautomatic structures. Additionally, we find that the boundary complex of a building mirrors the structure of a biautomatic space when associated with a uniform lattice. This conceptual framework allows us to prove the conjecture recently posed by Horbez and Velhøj regarding the biautomatic nature of the group of graph automorphisms acting on a building. Our proof relies on an extension of a previous theorem-established connection between the structure of a biautomatic group and the characteristics of a system of rays. A significant aspect of our proof involves verifying that the equicontinuity condition, as defined within the extended theorem, is satisfied for the group of graph automorphisms. We introduce the term "biautomatic boundary" to describe the relationship between a building's boundary and its set of directions, and we explore its implications further. Finally, we consider an example related to the general context of our theory. The results presented in this paper have implications for groups whose elements can be characterized by specific inversion patterns, properties of which can be mapped to the structure of a building. These groups, comprising discrete subgroups of isometry groups of buildings, will necessarily form biautomatic sets. Furthermore, we identify uniform lattices within the symmetry groups of buildings as additional instances of biautomatic groups. The foundations laid in this paper also provide a basis for investigating other potential biautomatic structures within the context of geometric group theory. The connection we establish between the field of graph automorphisms and biautomatic properties also gives rise to new research questions regarding the biautomatic nature of groups whose action on graphical structures defines a high-degree polynomial of the building type. Moreover, this relationship prompts exploration of the question of whether uniform lattices within the symmetry groups of high-dimensional polynomial structures also form biautomatic spaces. Lastly, this paper introduces an intriguing link between the theory of biautomatic groups and the famous Burnside problem, concerning the existence of non-trivial group actions under certain algebraic conditions, which further complicates the problem by adding another variable to the equation. This complication, however, does not affect groups within the class of abstract groups, as demonstrated by an accompanying proof. The proof relies on an extension of a previous theorem-established connection between the structure of a biautomatic group and the characteristics of a system of rays.

This paper presents events at an 2.76 TeV collision energy for Pb-Pb, derived from a set of parameters known as "event shapes," which quantify the directional distribution of energy and particle flow in heavy-ion collisions.  These events were generated using the JADE and Drell-Yan matrix elements within the PYTHIA 6 event generator and modified for heavy ions.  A customized analysis eliminated remnants of the collision zone and surrounding "halos" to isolate the central, most relevant portion.  Further adjustments were made to create "infrared-safe" observables that only consider energy transferred from particle interactions.  When comparing the resulting data to the same approach used for pp collisions at 7 TeV, a notable increase in the radius of elliptic motion in Pb-Pb collisions became apparent, aligning with existing findings from the ALICE and ATLAS experiments.  In contrast, the shape of the spectrum for the transverse momentum remained largely unchanged, raising implications for theoretical models that predict a distinct shift in shape and amplitude of the elliptic motion spectrum.  In addition, our results demonstrated that the choice of infrared-safe variables has a notable impact on the resulting spectrum in small-nucleon-scattering measurements.  Finally, our research provides a basis for further development of event generators and precision tests of theoretical models in heavy-ion collisions.  As such, we recommend the creation of public access to our custom-modified event generators for heavy ions, which integrate the JADE and Drell-Yan matrix elements within the PYTHIA 6 framework. Negation is a complex sentence element that numerous studies has been identified as a challenge for current natural language processing models. In order to enhance the ability of models to grasp negation correctly, this paper introduces CONDAQA, a comprehensive English reading comprehension dataset that is specifically designed to test a quad-partite hypothesis about negation. Diverse human annotators evaluated 1,584 text passages and labeled sections indicating the scope of the negation, and whether the negation has an explicit or implicit meaning, and whether the negation is restricted to a particular element of the text or not. Our initial findings confirm that both human annotators and automated models have difficulty understanding the scope of the negation, and that many models tend to overestimate the reach of the negation. To address this challenge, CONDAQA includes a set of challenging questions that are designed to be answered correctly only if the models can grasp the scope of the negation accurately. Our experiments demonstrate significant disparities in the performance of models when they are evaluated on standard SQuAD datasets versus CONDAQA, and therefore, we propose a new evaluation metric called Negation Scope Accuracy that takes into consideration the scope of the negation. This new metric yields striking results, and confirms our hypothesis that current state-of-the-art models are not yet capable of accurately understanding the scope of the negation. Our CONDAQA dataset, along with our experimental results, lays the foundation for further research on the understanding of complex sentence elements, and it is available at https://github.com/ParasSing7/CONDAQA, and is being incorporated into the standard reading comprehension evaluation benchmarks. One critical aspect that needs to be highlighted is the fact that modern transformer-based models have a tendency to overestimate the reach of the negation, and therefore, more research is needed to allow these models to accurately understand the scope of the negation. One possible direction for further research could be the incorporation of negation-specific attention mechanisms that are capable of grasping the scope of the negation accurately. However, incorporating such mechanisms would likely complicate the model even further, and therefore, it would be interesting to see if a more straightforward approach, such as adding a Negation Scope Accuracy criterion in the training objective, would be sufficient to address this challenge. Computing underlying structures in information networks is a complex task that requires a significant amount of storage and processing power. To address this, we propose a novel, scalable framework that utilizes a combination of distributed memory and processing resources to identify various structures, such as cliques, low-density subgraphs, and graphons, by dividing the graph into manageable chunks and processing them in an efficient, parallelized manner. This approach is particularly effective for analyses involving a large number of random variables, as it leverages the principles of structural learning and Bayesian networks. Our framework is highly versatile and can be easily integrated with existing optimization tools, such as message passing and SGD, to handle a wide range of objectives and constraints. To validate our approach, we conducted extensive experiments on real-world and synthetic graphs, demonstrating its ability to efficiently compute structures in networks with thousands of nodes and edges. Notably, our framework enabled us to compute graphons for datasets with up to 16,000 nodes, a significant improvement over existing methods. Our code is openly accessible on the PyStruct Networks website. Furthermore, we introduced an new version of the Cytoscape-Scala library, providing a more intuitive and user-friendly interface for working with large-scale graph datasets in Scala. This new version includes several innovative features, such as the ability to handle binary and weighted graphs, as well as the computation of various graph descriptors and structures. Additionally, we explored the integration of our framework with the Hadoop MapReduce architecture, a widely-used distributed processing environment. Our results show that our framework is highly compatible with Hadoop, but we encountered several scalability limitations with this approach. To overcome these challenges, we developed an alternative solution that leverages a hybrid memory architecture, combining the benefits of in-memory processing and disk-based storage to compute structures in large graphs. This new method, called the Hybrid Memory Structure Computation (HyMSc), offers a significant improvement in performance and is particularly well-suited for graphs with a large number of nodes and edges. To further improve the efficiency of our framework, we introduced an new technique that leverages a graph mini-mapping approach, reducing memory consumption and computation time by minimizing the amount of memory used to represent graph variables. This paper investigates the long-term behavior of a hard-sphere Boltzmann equation in an infinite space for initial data with minor fluctuations around a global equilibrium distribution. We demonstrate that under certain mild conditions on the initial data, the solution's distribution function will eventually conform to the phase-blending solution of a certain transport equation, which is equivalent to a Taylor diffusion equation. We also establish that the phase-blending solution consists of two distinct components: one that converges to the global equilibrium distribution and another that forms an oscillatory pattern in the velocity space. We establish the convergence rate of the distribution function to the phase-blending solution using an expanded velocity space and a new cancellation property of the gain matrix. We impose only a weak regularity condition on the potential interaction between spheres, unlike previous similar studies. This finding is verified through both formal asymptotic analysis and rigorous existence and uniqueness proof of the phase-blending solution. We derive an explicit formula for the transport equation's solution and its oscillatory component, which includes a velocity-smoothing effect and a nonlinear instability in the Boltzmann equation. This is the first time such a result has been obtained for the non-cutoff Boltzmann equation. This research is an extension of a previous study on the cutoff Boltzmann equation in a confined space with smooth boundaries. Our results show that the current model is too restrictive and needs to account for variations in the way waves interact with solar radiation over different time periods and across different areas of the ocean. In certain integrable models, solitons undergo a remarkable process called "recollision," where a soliton that has lost energy due to a collision with a breather or kink, suddenly experiences a significant increase in amplitude, resulting in a near complete recovery of its initial peak. This phenomenon is particularly evident in the Sine-Gordon model, where it leads to a substantial enhancement of the soliton's amplitude, rather than a decrease, following a collision with a breather. A distinct "recollision" effect is seen in the massive Dirac model, where a soliton that has lost momentum due to interacting with a soliton or kink-like object, will instead experience an increase in its momentum, returning it to its initial value. A key observation is that both the amplitude and momentum of the self-trapped wave will be enhanced by a specific amount, displaying a soliton "recollision" effect, where this increase is linked to the 12th root of the product of their initial and final values. A new self-trapped field theory, inspired by the massive Dirac model, is then presented, and it's shown that it possesses a self-trapped state with a breathertype structure, where the amplitude of this type of wave is continuously boosted by an amount that is directly proportional to the momentum of the wave, leading to an exponential increase in the amplitude. This new model is capable of producing a self-trapped state with a maximum amplitude, making it a model that self-activates and sustains self-trapped states. A note is made that both the massive Dirac model and the new self-trapped field theory have even-parity solutions, where the amplitude of the self-trapped state is boosted due to a self-trapped momentum mode, while the mass model's odd-parity solution, where the momentum of the self-trapped state is boosted due to a self-trapped amplitude mode, is shown to be unstable. A brief discussion is also provided on the potential applications of a self-trapped state with a breathertype structure in both atomic, mesoscopic, and optical systems. The Random Stroll method involves each participant creating a separate dataset with its own unique features, after which a model is trained on each dataset in an independent manner. Following this initial training, a model is learned from all the participants using the shared data and existing models as training examples. This learned model can then be used by the participants for their individual classification tasks. We compare this approach to traditional methods such as federated learning and multi-task learning through extensive experiments, and the results show that the Random Stroll method achieves comparable performance with significantly less communication between participants. The code for this study has been made available online. Moreover, a broader implication of this work is that it may offer insights on creating educational datasets through a game-like approach called the 4R method, which involves releasing relevant resources to students for their individual learning purposes. The 4R method is analogous to the 4R's of marketing, which are reach, relevance, two-way interaction, and return on investment, and our research on the Random Stroll method provides a real-world evidence for the effectiveness of the 4R approach in the context of education. Additionally, our research is also relevant to the study on the effect of diversity in models, and the results obtained from the experiments conducted in this study provide a solution to one of the open research questions. Furthermore, the results obtained from the experiments conducted in this study are also relevant to the evaluation of the education system in a real-world setting, and the findings from this study can be applied to the evaluation of the Microsoft's AI for Earth program. The paper is an extended version of a previous paper that was presented at the Federated Learning (FedLearn) workshop, which was co-organised by one of the authors at the Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (CVPR). The paper was also the top-performing paper at the FedLearn workshop challenge. Furthermore, the paper has been cited as a reference in multiple previous studies, and one of the authors is the recipient of the 2020 Early Career Award in Computer and Information Sciences from the University of Delaware. The paper has been viewed by over 5 million people, and the preprint paper has been downloaded over 50,000 times. The paper was also the subject of an interview with one of the authors by one of the premier technology news websites.

This study provides mathematical support for the previously observed Zakharov-Kolmogorov energy spectrum in the simulation of turbulent flows experiencing rotational constraints. The energy spectrum in such environments follows a specific pattern, with the energy quantitatively linked to the square of the wavenumber, indicating a clear relationship that can be expressed as $E(k) \propto k^3$. The underlying basis for this spectrum is the isotropic distribution of inertial wave velocities, which results from the natural limitations imposed by the rotation. In turn, this leads to the formation of a distinct curve in the bi-dimensional space of wavenumbers, giving rise to the $k^3$ component of the energy spectrum. The evidence for the Zakharov-Kolmogorov spectrum comes from both direct and indirect sources. The former includes the evaluation of energy flux and bi-spectral flux, as well as the examination of velocity probability distribution and structure functions. The latter is supported by the comparison with analytical models under controlled conditions, the exploration of the spectrum in different turbulence simulations, and the identification of an exact $k^3$ energy spectrum in one instance. The research with $f=0.1U$ is particularly noteworthy, where both direct and indirect approaches yield the same conclusion regarding the Zakharov-Kolmogorov spectrum. The findings of this study are relevant to various rotating fluid environments, such as planetary interiors and geophysical fluids, where the Zakharov-Kolmogorov spectrum may be applicable in the absence of geometric constraints and a critical Reynolds number. The criminal justice and mental health systems share a common goal: to rehabilitate and restore former offenders and individuals with mental illnesses back to productive members of society. This paper offers an academic exploration into the intersection of these two areas by examining the effect of mandatory therapy on individuals within the criminal justice system who struggle with mental wellness. We have conducted a thorough analysis of existing research within this domain, gathering insights from 22 studies and 13 experts within the field. Our empirical data reveals that, regardless of the disorder, participating in the recovery process has a positive impact, whereas not engaging with treatment yields unfavorable outcomes. Furthermore, experts concur that recovery is more likely to occur when offenders are given the opportunity to reflect on their past actions and take personal responsibility for their conduct. Additionally, the following factors were identified as influencing the effectiveness of treatment: the expertise of treatment providers, the environment within correctional facilities, and the presence of support networks for both individuals with mental health conditions and correctional officers. Building upon these findings and incorporating elements from the Theory of Planned Behavior, we have developed a comprehensive framework that explains the decision-making process involved in participating in treatment, as well as the factors that either support or hinder this process. This model can be applied across various mental health disorders within the criminal justice system and may serve as a foundation for designing more effective interventions and treatments. Ultimately, our research underscores the critical role that assessment, tailoring, and a supportive environment play in facilitating participation in treatment, as well as the importance of addressing the underlying causes of an individual's criminal behavior in order to restore their mental wellness and promote a more constructive outlook. This, in turn, can contribute to a reduction in recidivism rates and an increased likelihood of successful community reintegration. This integrated approach can also serve as an illustration for the integration of mental health and criminal justice systems, showcasing how recovery-oriented language and practices can be incorporated across both domains. This, in turn, may promote a more harmonious and collaborative relationship between these systems, with a shared focus on the rehabilitation and restoration of individuals with mental health conditions within the criminal justice system. This, in turn, may, in turn, contribute to a more seamless transition for these individuals as they navigate both systems, with potential positive outcomes for both the mental health and criminal justice systems as a whole. realistic avatar visualization and pose detection. These vectors not only enable
the avatars to be accurately positioned within real-world scenes but also
facilitate realistic skin rendering. However, traditional methods rely on internal
states within the neural renderer and estimating these states from raw images
proves challenging, especially when attempting to capture complex articulations.
We introduce a novel approach, referred to as Articulated Neural Rendering
(ANR), which treats the articulation as a compositional component and treats the
skin rendering as a task of image-to-image translation. ANR training involves a
two-step process: training a pose estimator and subsequent training of a pose
conditioned neural renderer on synthetic images generated by a separate trainer
of a pose generator. We also introduce an extended version of the widely
used Novel View Synthesis (NVS) benchmark, referred to as NVS+, which
demonstrates ANR's superiority over existing methods. Furthermore, we show that
ANR's models generalizable and multiple such models can be trained with little
expense, also demonstrating the robustness of ANR. ANR code and data can be
found at https://github.com/yashengwang/anr. We hope this research to pave the
way for the development of realistic avatar-based applications. We have created a
video showcasing our research findings and approach at https://youtube.com/... and
have presented this research at the 31st British Machine Conference. In addition
to improved results on NVS+, ANR's unique design also prevents the leakage of
external information, and unlike memory-based approaches, ANR's models are easy
to interpret and there is no issue with spatial coherence. Additionally, ANR is
efficient as it only requires the generation of synthetic images during training
and not the creation of complex internal states. We believe this research will
be of use to developers working on avatar-based projects that utilize deep
learning techniques. We have created multiple animations that illustrate the
realistic avatars rendered by ANR at https://youtube.com/... and have made the
extended NVS benchmark results for the average and standard deviation of all

In this research, a novel approach to understanding and explaining network predictions is presented, based on applying graph attention models to neural networks. This involves training a neural network to predict the behavior of a trapped atomodain system and using this prediction in the learning algorithm of a controller. Our findings reveal that the closure of the set of operators related to $P$, denoted as $\overline{R_P}$, is equal to the set of all elliptic operators on $T\mathcal{X}$, provided $P$ is not identically equal to the Laplace-Beltrami operator and does not have a constant characteristic polynomial. As mobile devices continuously update models via federated learning, asynchronous uploads can result in performance variations, prompting clients to wait for other users to update models before sending their own changes. To overcome this issue, clients can employ a cache system to store gradient calculations until a predetermined deadline, thereby filling existing asynchronous federated learning frameworks with support for unconstrained gradients and variable update frequencies. Through the proposed approach, clients can calculate gradients at any time, update models independently, and send accumulated batches to the server, reducing performance losses due to asynchronous data collection. Simulation results demonstrate that unconstrained gradients can be calculated more efficiently than constrained ones, and this approach is particularly beneficial for slow clients, increasing overall aggregation efficiency up to 9.5% in certain scenarios. Furthermore, our method proves more effective than existing solutions in scenarios with a wide range of client update frequencies, reducing loss rates by up to 13.8%. The proposed approach is readily integratable with existing federated learning frameworks and only requires the incorporation of a buffer module, along with modifications to client and server algorithms. The newly introduced buffer module can be viewed as an extension of the async-FedAvg framework, with our approach now being the default method of operation. The newly proposed buffer module is comprised of a first-in-first-out queue with a fixed capacity, responsible for storing gradient calculations from mobile devices until a predetermined deadline, after which it computes an unconstrained mini-batch by selecting the most up-to-date elements from the buffer. The implemented algorithm, known as Buffered Asynchronous Accumulation (BAA), can be viewed as a direct outcome of combining the async-FedAvg framework with the proposed buffer module, resulting in an unconstrained gradient accumulation approach. The theoretical analysis of BAA reveals that it can be viewed as an optimization of the FedAvg algorithm, with the option to process historical gradient calculations. The novel approach to processing historical gradient calculations can be viewed as increasing the effective mini-batch size, with the benefit of reducing the influence of stale gradients, with BAA being an optimal solution for slow clients. The results of extensive simulations, carried out on diverse datasets and networks, serve as a comprehensive evaluation of the BAA algorithm, with the obtained conclusions highly relevant to the broader field of federated learning. The practical implications of the proposed approach, along with the theoretical contributions and the comprehensive evaluation, make a significant contribution to the development of innovative solutions for the optimization of federated learning. This conclusion comes from observing $B^0$ and ${\kern.3em} \overline{\kern -.7em B\kern.3em }}\kern -.3em ^{0}$ decays behave differently under CP transformation. Additionally, our study suggests that the recorded state $f_X(1500)$ in $B\to \eta(K)KK$ decays originates from the product of $\rho^0(1450)$ and an residual resonance. Furthermore, our study predicts $\rho^0(1450)$ can be detected in two-sideband method for the quasicolar $B\to \eta\eta$ decays. Moreover, the recorded state $f_X(1500)$ in $B\to \eta\eta$ decays comes from the combination of $\rho^0(1450)$ and a scalar state with mass around $1000$ MeV. The properties of this state cannot be determined due to a lack of relevant information. The Shadow Dimension hypothesis proposes that our universe has a parallel dimension where dark matter exists as an external, rather than internal, reality. This results in a universe with no true dark matter field. To account for the typical dark matter density, the hypothesis requires the existence of primordial black holes (PBHs) of a specific mass range. We calculate the most likely range of PBH masses based on their overall density and find it to be between $10^{15}$ and $10^{17}$ grams. We then analyze various phenomena related to PBHs, such as their formation from gravitational waves and the merging of small PBHs, which could also produce primordial gravitational waves. We also calculate the expected abundance of sub-millimeter sized PBHs, which could interact with regular matter only during the early universe when matter and radiation densities were comparable. We explore the possibility of these small PBHs being responsible for the observed variations in cosmic ray short-term flux. We also discuss the possibility of the Dark Energy Swampland, which could be addressed by introducing a scalar field with a high potential that could be reached by a primordial inflationary field. This could result in a universe with a dark energy density similar to its initial conditions. We estimate the required energy scale for this process to occur and find it to be on the order of $10^{15}$ GeV. We then discuss several on-going and future experiments and surveys that will significantly improve our understanding of the physical properties of PBHs. We also discuss the implications of detecting or dismissing the existence of PBHs, as well as the potential for solving the Dark Matter Problem, and potentially the Dark Energy Problem, if their existence is confirmed. We've analyzed a range of SU(Nc) gauge theories in 3D lattices that incorporate complex, multi-component scalar fields, which are linked by a variety of interactions that can be adjusted with distinct parameters. These interactions are modeled after a general potential that is compatible with the symmetries present in the 3D lattice, thus enabling the incorporation of multiple exact symmetry-breaking phases. Depending on the specific conditions, the scalar fields may either stabilize the discrete symmetry-breaking phase or transition into a phase that breaks the symmetry in a manner consistent with the Higgs mechanism. We've derived the phase diagrams for several combinations of interacting potentials, some of which feature Higgs states with masses determined by both the gauge and scalar masses, as well as the number of symmetry-breaking parameters. Additionally, we've observed distinct modes of Higgs instability in both the discrete and continuous symmetry-breaking phases, and we've identified various regimes of Higgs state formation on both the charge condensation and superfluid phases. Galactic magnetic fields are recognized as a vital component in the study of galaxy evolution, however their precise impact on the development of galaxies in an evolving universe remains unclear. This study presents a suite of high-resolution, multi-scale simulations of galaxy formation in an expanding universe, with magnetic fields strengthened to the observed strengths in present-day galaxies. The effects on structure and star formation within these galaxies were analyzed and compared to their non-magnetic counterparts through an extensive set of scaling laws. In general, the amplified magnetic fields were found to suppress fragmentation in gas and star formation within the galactic disks, reducing their scale and enhancing their central density. The enhanced magnetic fields caused gas disks to fragment into curved, spiral-shaped filaments, with rotation curves indicating increased angular momentum conservation. This, in turn, led to slower star formation rates across the disks and a shift in the mass-to-light ratios of the galaxies. The impact of these magnetic fields on the rates of major galaxy mergers was found to be insignificant, with mergers occurring at a rate 5% higher than in their non-magnetic counterparts, though this increase seemed to be caused by the tighter binding of gas and stellar disks rather than increased towards-convergence interactions. The results of these simulations contradict the widely-held assumption that amplified magnetic fields suppress gas flow during galaxy mergers, with actual effects depending on the specific features of the merging galaxies. The implications of these findings for the expected outcomes of galaxy mergers in more detailed simulations are discussed in a companion paper. The enhanced magnetic fields used in these simulations may not be sufficient to create the observed large-scale magnetic field patterns in galaxies, with further studies needed to determine the effects of wider, filament-like magnetic field structures on galaxy mergers. The effects seen in these simulations may also be too great, with further research needed to determine the precise impact of magnetic fields on galaxy mergers. Most current Grammatical Error Rectification (GER) research focuses on a single domain, utilizing extensively labeled data for training. In reality, GER applications often involve adapting to new domains with limited resources. This paper explores a novel few-shot domain transfer GER model, leveraging meta-learning to optimize adaptations for multiple new domains using only a small amount of data from each. This approach allows our model to effectively utilize a small set of inter-domain relations, thereby facilitating transfers between more diverse domains. Notably, our model's performance in each new domain is evaluated as equivalent to a model trained on a full dataset for that domain. In experiments, our model achieves comparable performance to a model trained on extensive domain-specific data when targeting simple errors but outperforms models trained on targeted data when correcting more complex errors, especially those involving multiple issues. Furthermore, our model's ability to learn from various reference responses in each new domain ensures more accurate performances. In total, we complete 16 challenging few-shot domain transfer GER tasks across 4 available datasets, a first in the field. Our code and data are openly accessible at https://github.com/ghrua/few-shot-ger. In summary, our few-shot domain transfer GER research paves the way for developing more adaptable and interdomain Ger models. In particular, our model's capability to learn from various reference responses in each new domain ensures more accurate performances. This research is significant because it indicates that meta-learning can be highly effective for a task like Ger, especially when targeting more complex errors. Furthermore, our research highlights potential applications of meta-learning in other writing-related tasks like style transfer and text generation. In such situations, models trained with meta-learning tend to perform better than models trained with standard optimization methods on existing datasets. This is because models trained with standard optimization methods often overfit the data from the source domain, resulting in underperforming on the target domain. Researchers and surveyors often collect data rounded to the nearest integer, leading to uncertainty in calculated totals. Typically, these rounds are thought to be equally distributed between adjacent numbers, but in certain situations, especially when respondents are unsure or estimate difficult values, there may be a bias towards rounding up or down. Considering such factors can affect estimates of totals and proportions, we first review existing research on rounding behavior, emphasizing the importance of accounting for ambiguity when interpreting data. We then discuss standard statistical methods that assume no bias exists and explore alternative approaches to estimating totals and proportions under ambiguous data, ultimately recommending the use of the median instead. We also provide a general framework for processing data subject to various types of bias and suggest potential directions for future research in this area. We apply our findings to an existing data set and present a R function for conducting the analysis presented in this article. The task of allocating essential items among self-interested agents, who make rational decisions to maximize their own value, has been extensively examined in the field of algorithmic game theory. In contrast to routine tasks like sorting or matching, allocating these items can be an complex and challenging process. Building on the classic model proposed by Kelso and Crawford, we introduce a new framework for allocating a range of items among multiple agents, who submit their preferred orders and engage in a strategic bidding process. Our equilibrium analysis, which focuses on pure Nash equilibria, reveals that the social welfare may not be optimized through efficient allocations presented to the agents as take-it-or-leave-it offers. Moreover, the distribution of these equilibria may not align with fair outcomes like envy-free or propotional fairness. Building on these negative findings, we explore design options for allocating items among selfish agents in a more collaborative manner, examining the impact of various rules on the set of possible equilibria and their associated fairness characteristics. Our findings include a characterizations of equitable allocations that are resistant to all pure Nash equilibria, as well as a discussion on the effect of introducing price mechanisms or bidding fees in the context of our general item allocation framework. Ultimately, our research provides novel insights on the equity of pure Nash equilibria in the general item allocation setting, a topic that was first introduced by Kleinberg, Leymarie, and Mahdawijaha in their paper on the allocation of discrete items. That paper considered a specific item allocation problem, known as the 'round-display advertising problem', in which a seller allocates ads to users who, in turn, engage in a strategic sorting process. Our research extends and generalizes many of the design options and fairness guarantees that were presented in that paper. In our research, we diverge from the standard approach in unsupervised domain adaptation (UDA) that relies on a direct, deterministic transformation from the source to target domain. Instead, we allow a stochastic transformation to accommodate the inevitable differences between domains. This shift enables us to develop novel methods for adjusting domains beyond the conventional, deterministic strategy. Specifically, we introduce two new strategies: one that utilizes a source proxy to refine the target data and another that leverages a target auxiliary to refine the source data. Both proposals are straightforward to execute, requiring only minor adjustments to existing prototype-based protocols. Our experiments validate the benefits of stochastic transformations, resulting in superior performance compared to the conventional approach in multiple domains across three different datasets and protocols. Notably, our results show improved performance in complex scenarios involving large domain gaps. Minimally invasive surgery has emerged as a highly effective treatment, allowing for non-invasive exploration and treatment of abdominal pathologies. Advances in medical technology, particularly high-definition cameras and sophisticated software, have enhanced its efficacy and safety. However, tool detection and tracking algorithms can cause delays, hindering safe execution of the procedure. Currently available datasets and leading deep learning-based tools fall short of providing precise and timely results. In response, we've introduced two novel datasets featuring 3D meshes and 2D annotations for further development and evaluation of deep learning-based tools. Our research incorporates three well-known deep learning-based tools - ENet, ENet with EN-Criterion, and BiSeNet - and assesses their performance using the introduced datasets. Notably, BiSeNet achieved exceptional results, surpassing existing benchmarks with superior accuracy and processing speed. Furthermore, our analysis revealed that BiSeNet's simplicity and optimal feature extraction contribute to its success. As a result, we recommend BiSeNet as the premier choice for real-time and precise segmentation of surgical tools during laparoscopy. Additionally, we observed that reducing precision requirements allows for the achievement of even faster processing times. This, in turn, could enable the integration of real-time tracking into safe tool use detection systems. Overall, our research provides a definitive comparison of deep learning-based tools and a new benchmark for the field, while also showcasing the value of collaborative research between medical and technical experts. In conclusion, we highlight the scope for further innovation in this area with the potential to create more sophisticated tools and to explore new applications for deep learning in medical robotics. Offline multi-agent reinforcement learning is crucial for developing safe and efficient robotic systems by leveraging previously collected data. However, existing offline methods have limitations such as requiring individual agent expert trajectories or relying on expensive online learning with high-quality data, which isn't always feasible. This research introduces an innovative algorithm called PTRA, an offline method for learning from just positive trajectories in collaborative multi-agent scenarios. The algorithm first identifies a collaborative policy using only observations from interacting agents, and then uses this information to estimate an individual agent's optimal response. It then formulates the learning task as a series of bi-directional reinforcement learning problems with shared memory, and leverages the expertise within each agent's history of trajectories to overcome the distribution shift. The proposed framework also allows the learning of multiple agent roles by factoring in shared skills through a multi-tasking approach. The results show that PTRA outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods on real-world tasks, including a complex kitchen scenario, by successfully learning from just positive trajectories in real-world scenarios with over 10 million data steps. Megavoltage imaging is a technique that provides detailed information about tissue density in patients undergoing radiation therapy. However, MV images are commonly acquired with low resolution and poor contrast, which can make aligning them with charge-coupled device images for treatment delivery challenging. Our research involves a Convolutional Neural Network in a task of aligning low-resolution MV images with higher-resolution CCDS images, achieving a registration error of 1.6 ± 0.4 pixels when evaluated against 11 test cases by multiple radiation therapy specialists. This compares favorably to traditional alignment methods and other state-of-the-art techniques. Furthermore, our team found that applying this registration technique to 3D volumes resulted in an accuracy comparable to that of 2D methods. Additionally, we investigated common artifacts found in MV images and discovered that a Convolutional Neural Network is capable of distinguishing real alignment errors from those caused by artifacts. This research lays the groundwork for further exploration of artifactual images and can contribute to developing artifactual-free megavoltage image sets, which could standardize the process of radiation therapy delivery. This in turn could lead to more consistent treatment outcomes across different facilities. Our research also provides a foundation for exploring other applications involving the registration of different imaging modalities. Furthermore, our research can contribute to the development of open-source software for analyzing and enhancing the quality of low-resolution megavoltage images. FL, an emerging field that enables collaborative model training without exchanging data, has given rise to the development of several FL-based IoVs solutions. A comprehensive literature review on the topic has been conducted, resulting in a total of 80 sources included in this review, with all entries properly cited. Multi-user MIMO is a technology that can improve performance in such scenarios, but its efficiency depends on effective codebook design and feedback encoding, especially considering the high overhead associated with exchanging feedback information in FDD systems. To address this challenge, we developed an alternative approach to codebook design and feedback encoding, based on statistical estimation and a codebook search process. Our solution utilizes Gaussian mixture models to represent the channel correlation and perform codebook optimization, reducing the number of required references by up to 75%. We also designed a feedback encoding algorithm that leverages a hierarchical codebook structure and reduces the amount of exchanged information by as much as 50%. Simulation results showed that our proposed solution delivers performance gains of up to 20 db in terms of spectral efficiency in scenarios with multiple users and spatially correlated channels. Furthermore, our scheme is robust and capable of handling a wide range of channel conditions, achieving only a limited loss in efficiency when compared to ideal, reference-based approaches. To facilitate practical codebook development, we created an open-access codebook design toolkit available online for users to customize and optimize codebooks for various use cases and channel scenarios. Overall, our proposed approach delivers enhanced performance, reduces complexity, and offers a more sustainable solution to the codebook design and feedback encoding problem in FDD systems. We believe our solution can serve as a codebook design foundation for other applications and systems. By using GRB data, researchers can train machine learning models to predict the energy and duration of future GRBs. This would be especially useful for the Gamma-Ray Burst Alert Detector and Gamma-Ray Burst Directory Engine (GECAM), which relies on GRB duration and energy information to locate and analyze GRBs. In this paper, a portable Gamma-Ray Burst emulator called PGRB, based on the scikit-learn dataset API, is created to facilitate the development of such models by allowing custom datasets and models to be used. PGRB's performance is evaluated using various models and datasets, including the standard LIGO gravitational wave detector strain data and custom datasets constructed from real and synthetic GRB data. By using a diverse range of features and physiological units, including luminosity and spectral characteristics, PGRB demonstrates its capability to accurately predict future GRBs through various performance metrics such as mean absolute error and precision. Furthermore, PGRB is designed to be portable by integrating multiple automated setup configurations, including optimized hyperparameters and a simplified interface for easy model selection. This makes PGRB an ideal tool for the detection and analysis of GRBs, particularly for space-based detectors like GECAM, by providing a reliable and efficient means of predicting and refining the performance of these bursts. In addition to its practical applications, PGRB's training and validation process involve a novel use of multiple real and synthetic gravitational wave detector strain data, making it a valuable resource for the broader physics community. By using this script, users can easily create their own custom datasets by incorporating their preferred data and scaling factors. This level of customizability, combined with PGRB's automated setup and easy model selection interface, makes PGRB an extremely useful tool for any team involved in the detection and analysis of GRBs, particularly those using the GECAM detectors. To better comprehend these issues, a study was conducted involving arXiv.org, one of the leading electronic preprint archives, where research articles on physics are published. A custom-made framework was developed to evaluate the relevance and redundancy of articles and estimate the underlying distribution of the information space. Experimental results indicate a trade-off between performance and energy consumption in this solution. Ultimately, this research has verified the practical viability of this error detection and recovery method, which could potentially enable the development of reliable neural networks for various applications using analog computing. The concept of set-off, a legal mechanism allowing firms to eliminate debts owed to each other, simplifies debt resolution by minimizing monetary transfers. This process involves solving a system of linear equations representing inter-firm transactions, where the variables are the monetary payments made between firms. We present an innovative algorithm based on graph theory, specifically node disintegration, for resolving set-off. This algorithm ensures optimal results by minimizing payment amounts, which can then be further minimized by an alternative approach. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our algorithm by applying it to a real-world scenario from the Romanian Ministry of Finance. This involves a scenario with approximately 150,000 variables and 170 million equations, as well as a simulated scenario with over 13 million variables and 130 billion equations. Our algorithm produces results that can be interpreted and visually represented using a range of parameters, including the number of nodes in the graph and the payment standards. These payment standards, which determine the amount paid in each node, can also be set dynamically. We also explore different solutions provided by the algorithm and its components, including a method for confirming the optimality of the solution. This confirmation involves a series of checks, or certifications, associated with each node in the graph, where a node represents a group of firms that can pay each other in full. We demonstrate our algorithm using a scenario from the Romanian Ministry of Finance, which involved a significant debt of over RON 3 billion, or approximately EUR 650 million, and showed that the algorithm can reduce the required payments by an additional RON 200 million, or about EUR 42 million, in addition to the initial RON 300 million, or about EUR 64 million, already settled through set-off. This resulted in a total reduction of over RON 500 million, or approximately EUR 106 million, in the debts owed. We also explore the computational time of the algorithm, which can be quite complex, especially in larger cases, and discuss a few aspects that can be optimized, such as the ordering of the firms. The framework pre-trains a model using the annotated dataset and then subjects it to contrastive semi-supervised learning constraints during dense sampling of the unannotated dataset. In 1992, Gelfand and MacPherson established an intriguing connection between the Pontrjagin classes of a manifold and the invariant coefficients of a specific universal differential operator. This differential operator, known as the universal differential operator, is constructed from a manifold's de Rham differential via pullback and composition with various functions. The crux of their approach lies in showing that the Pontrjagin classes can be expressed as the preimages of these invariant coefficients under the composition with the map induced by the universal differential operator. Our work delves deeper into this relationship by examining the coefficients of the pullback of the universal differential operator on a manifold's singular set. We demonstrate that these coefficients contain valuable information about the Pontrjagin classes of the manifold's singular set. Furthermore, we establish a link between the Pontrjagin classes of a manifold and its singular set by illustrating that the differences between the Pontrjagin classes of a manifold and those of its singular set are captured by the coefficients of the pullback of the universal differential operator on the singular set. This extension of the Gelfand-MacPherson formula provides a connection between the Pontrjagin classes of a manifold and its singular set in the context of differential forms. Additionally, we discuss how this relationship between the Pontrjagin classes of a manifold and its singular set is reflected through the use of motivic integrals. This is illustrated by a concrete example involving the calculation of the volume of a singular differential form on a manifold. We also investigate how this connection between the Pontrjagin classes of a manifold and its singular set can be expressed in terms of Milnor's volume function, which a leading geometers has made available to us in an unpublished form. This connection between the Pontrjagin classes of a manifold and its singular set holds significant value in the field of geometry and has implications for further research in the area. The detection of gravitational waves by the LIGO/VIRGO collaboration opens up a new field of study, allowing for the analysis of multimodal data resulting from complex astrophysical events. However, manual examination of all detected gravitational waves by humans is impractically expensive given the current detection rate. Therefore, an automated system that leverages deep learning and identifies promising targets for human inspection among the numerous detected signals is crucial. This paper presents a prototype of such an automated system, which utilizes a deep learning approach known as WaveNet, to classify the detections made by the LIGO/VIRGO collaboration into four categories of neutron star-black hole collisions based on their morphology. The model's effectiveness is demonstrated through its performance on a dataset of 114 detected gravitational waves, achieving a classification accuracy of 98.25%. This marks the first instance of a deep learning model successfully classifying the morphological characteristics of neutron star-black hole collision events using the detections made by a gravitational wave detector. This technique has the potential to be expanded to other types of neutron star-black hole collision events and other gravitational wave detectors, streamlining the process of discovering new phenomena and reducing costs. The model's code has been made publicly available on the GitHub repository identified as https://github.com/stratus-ai/gravitational-waves. This is the first instance such code of has been shared publicly. Furthermore, the model has been successfully applied to the detection of neutron star-black hole collisions as part of the third observing run by the LIGO/VIRGO collaboration. This is the first instance a deep learning-based approach has been deployed in conjunction with the collaboration's detection pipeline. On 1st September 2021, the model identified the neutron star-black hole merger event that occurred 11 days prior, demonstrating the effectiveness of this technology in the real-world application of gravitational wave detection. This has paved the way for the collaboration to consider integrating this type of deep learning-based approach into its detection pipeline during its upcoming observing runs. This paper has been submitted to the IEEE Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (CVPR) 2020. Due to the conference restrictions, the paper has been withdrawn from consideration and the code has been made available on the GitHub repository identified as https://github.com/stratus-ai/gravitational-waves. This model has been recognized as one of the top 10 projects in the 2020 PyTorch Metadata Paper Competition. On 29rd September 2021, the model was presented at the PyTorch Metadata Paper Competition Workshop
