In the context of dependent types, the normalization function serves as both a type checker and a proof verifier. However, the development of a normalization function for the Dependent Type Theory (DTT) was long considered an unsolved problem. A breakthrough was made possible by the inclusion of dependent product types and functions into the type theory, which was first achieved for the Calculus of Constructions (CoC). This extension, referred to as the Extended Calculus of Constructions (ECoC), enables the development of a normalization function for its base theory. This paper builds upon earlier work by Chawatanon and Matsuoka, which demonstrated the possibility of creating a normalization function for the ECoC by incorporating robust normalization into the syntax. This approach allows the normalization function to be developed for the DTT by leveraging the normalization of the CoC's dependent product types and functions. This paper delves deeper into the details of this technique, referring to it as 'robust normalization,' which can be applied to any DTT with product types and functions. The paper then focuses on the application of this technique to the DTT underlying Agda, a popular proof assistant. By incorporating robust normalization into Agda's DTT, the development of a normalization function for Agda's types becomes possible. This, in turn, raises the type-checking of Agda's types to the level of the CoC. This enhanced type-checking includes the checking of againts, a condition related to the session polynomial types, which was recently introduced into Agda by Malmqvist and Spadola. The resulting type-checking provides a more secure form of type checking, which is, however, less efficient than the current method used in Agda. This study provides a detailed explanation for the recent discovery reported in \cite{Garraffo:2018}, which indicates that approximately 90\% of solar-type main sequence stars possess a stable magnetic field, whereas only about 10\% remain stable with an unstable magnetic field. We offer a mathematical expression that characterizes magnetic energy stability in stars, based on an ideal magnetic flux tube model. This ideal tube model ignores interactions with the surrounding star matter. Although this simplification may seem limited in comparison to leading magnetic flux tube models, which account for interactions with the star's matter, those models are only applicable to solar-like flux tubes. In contrast, our approach is relevant to stars with non-solar mass-to-magnetic flux ratios. We demonstrate that stable magnetic energy in stars depends on their internal structure, specifically the temperature structure within their hydrogen-burning zone, and we propose a universal temperature-radius relationship for stars with stable magnetic energy. Furthermore, we outline a method for predicting universal stable magnetic energy prototypes and discuss future directions for further investigation. Additionally, we address potential connections between a star's internal structure and its exterior magnetic field patterns. Last, we note the suitability of our approach for stars with non-solar mass-to-magnetic flux ratios and suggest that the proposed temperature-radius relationship may be used as an indicator of a star's internal stability. We also explore the possibility that the discovered universal relationship between temperature and radius within the hydrogen-burning zone may be an indicator of a star's internal stability, and discuss the use of this relationship in identifying unstable stars. Lastly, we provide an explanation for the abundance of bipolar protostars, suggesting that the discovered universal relationship could be an indicator of a protostar's internal instability, which may lead to the observed bipolar pattern. We propose that protostars passing through the hydrogen-burning stage may have their internal instability removed, resulting in a unipolar field pattern similar to that found in main sequence stars. We also consider the possibility that the recently discovered pairs of magnetic field loops in the protostar VV Ser during its T Tauri stage may be an evidence of its internal instability during that stage. We discuss how the discovered universal temperature-radius relationship may be used as an indicator of a protostar's or star's internal instability, and suggest future directions for further investigation. We also consider the possibility that the recently discovered pairs of magnetic field loops in the protostar VV Ser during its T Tauri stage may be an evidence of its internal instability during that stage.

In the first part of our study, we examine the applicability and predictive power of these quantitative fluid dynamics equations in the context of zero-dimensional quantum field theories, using the $O(N)$ model as a fundamental test case. Our comprehensive analysis involves an in-depth examination of the parametric region of the $O(N)$ model, which enables us to distinguish between fundamental branches of the theory and separate critical and non-critical dimensions. Furthermore, we demonstrate the capability of the FRG-based approach to describe cross-overs between fundamental fixed points and accurately determine critical exponents in two-dimensional $O(N)$ models, a task that has been a subject of debate in the physics literature. Music theory education is a historical field that has been revitalized in recent years through the application of AI techniques. Despite the many advancements in music education assisted by technology, there is still a lack of engaging and interactive tools to help students understand fundamental music concepts. To address this gap, we present Pied Piper, a cutting-edge AI-powered learning platform that utilizes a innovative meta-inquiry approach to present music theory in an interactive and immersive way. Pied Piper is an omnichannel educator that can be accessed through both website and mobile app interfaces, using various exercises and activities to help students grasp music theory principles. Additionally, Pied Piper includes a dedicated dashboard for tracking student progress and managing class activities. What sets Pied Piper apart from other music education tools is its unique meta-inquiry framework, which encourages students to explore music concepts through self-directed exploration and discovery. With Pied Piper, students can explore a wide range of music theory topics, from basic rhythm and melody to advanced harmony and composition. One of the key features of Pied Piper is its ability to generate personalized learning paths for each student, based on their individual performance and progress. This is achieved through the integration of multiple optimization techniques, including reinforcement learning, neural networks, and collaborative filtering. With its engaging meta-inquiry approach and advanced personalized learning technology, Pied Piper has the potential to revolutionize music theory education and make it more enjoyable and effective for both students and teachers. With further development, Pied Piper can also be extended to other subjects and learning domains, such as programming, foreign languages, and mathematics. With the rise of AI-powered learning platforms like Pied Piper, the traditional role of the teacher as the primary source of knowledge is being redefined, and the classroom of the future will be a collaborative learning environment where the teacher acts as a guide and Pied Piper serves as a dedicated facilitator. With its innovative meta-inquiry framework and advanced personalized learning technology, Pied Piper is poised to play a significant role in shaping the future of education. With the support of the Stanford Center for Biomedical Informatics, Pied Piper has been successfully tested with over 500 students and has shown significant improvements in student engagement and music theory understanding. With further refinement and a broader rollout, Pied Piper has the potential to become the leading music education platform, used by millions of students worldwide. We define a new concept called a geometric framework over a smooth manifold or stack, and demonstrate its utility by showing it's an appropriate setting for a broadened version of the concept of Dirac structure. This enhanced version removes the requirement on Poisson manifolds that their leaf spaces be orbit type. We then establish a connection between geometric frameworks and a type of differential graded module. Specifically, we prove that there is a bi-functorial relationship between the category of geometric frameworks and a specific category of differential graded modules. This relationship gives rise to the category of geometric frameworks as a subcategory of the category of differential graded modules. We also identify a full subcategory of differential graded modules that is equivalent to the category of geometric frameworks. This result is a key contribution of this work. Another key contribution is the demonstration that the category of geometric frameworks is a stacky version of the category of Dirac structures. This is further supported by an examination of the basic objects within the category of geometric frameworks, which includes showing that the underlying manifold of a geometric framework can be a non-orientable surface, such as the real projective plane, and that the leaf space of a geometric framework with an orientable underlying manifold is a differentiable stack. We also demonstrate that the category of geometric frameworks contains objects that can not be captured by the category of Dirac structures, which further highlights the value of introducing the concept of a geometric framework. Finally, we demonstrate that the concept of a geometric framework can be used to describe the underlying structure of a type of physical system known as a mechanical system, which is then followed by a discussion on possible future research in this area. We also define a new type of object called a super mechanical system, which is based on the concept of a geometric framework, and demonstrate that it is a stacky version of a mechanical system. We then conclude by summarizing the results presented in this thesis and outlining the scope of each chapter. We also include an appendix with additional details on the results presented in this thesis, which includes a lemma that was used in the proof of a theorem presented in this thesis, as well as a description of the software that was developed as part of this research. This software can be used to verify the results presented in this thesis, which includes a set of data that was used in a theorem presented in this thesis. We also include a description of the methodology that was used to develop this software, which includes a custom compiler that was developed in this research. We conclude this appendix by outlining the future directions

A detailed analysis of the Dragon infrared dark nebula, a complex molecular cloud, reveals an irregular, tripartite structure. This division may indicate three separate rotating core regions within the nebula. By comparing their characteristics to data from the Galactic Plane Survey, we found one of these components to have a similar spectral properties to the Sgr B2 complex. In addition, a 1.1 GHz VLA observation of the nebula revealed two discrete core regions, here referred to as core A and core B, with sizes of approximately 10.5 pc and 7.5 pc in diameter respectively, and mass-to-gas ratios of around 0.031 and 0.021 in units of (10^3 K km^2 pc^2)^-1. A temperature analysis, using H2O maser velocities as a guide, revealed temperatures of 40-50 K in both core A and core B, and an estimated total mass for the nebula of around 1.4 10^6 solar masses. A stability analysis using the Toomre criterion indicated that core B is more stable and less likely to fragment, while core A, more susceptible to fragmentation, may be on the path to forming massive stars. Core B, with its higher density and likelihood of forming smaller to intermediate-sized stars, may eventually become a high-mass star-forming region within the Dragon nebula. This, however, could still change if the nebula is impacted by an external gravitational force. Furthermore, the Dragon infrared dark nebula may be on the early stages of becoming a giant molecular association, like the Sagittarius B2 complex, through the accumulation of nearby molecular clouds. This could also be an indication that the nebula is being affected by an external gravitational force, one that is shaping the Sagittarius B2 complex as well as the Dragon infrared dark nebula in the direction of the Galactic Center. This, however, still needs further analysis and consideration of other scenarios. A 1.6 GHz follow-up observation of the water masers in the Dragon infrared dark nebula, added mass constraints and revealed an estimated total mass for the nebula of around 1.7 10^6 solar masses, in addition to providing more detailed information on the morphology of the water masers within the nebula, here referred to as the North and South components, as well as a third, recently discovered, mini-core within the South area. Godel modal logics can be regarded as an extension of traditional Godel logics with modal operators added to the framework. This family of modal logics arises when the normality condition is relaxed for intuitionistic logic-based modal operators. Our research offers a novel approach, grounded in relational semantics, to the Godel modal logics and its expansions. We introduce a semi-completeness theorem for the basic Godel modal logic in the context of both finite and infinite algebras and structures, building on a notion of truth preservation. Additionally, we demonstrate that certain axioms can be derived from the applicable types of finite structures, resulting in a combination of algebraic and relational semantics for the Godel modal logics. This research provides a starting point for the exploration of hybrid structures combining features from both the Godel and Heyting algebras. Our results can also be applied to the prelinearity property, a notion recently introduced in the context of Godel logic-based modal operators. We demonstrate that the property of prelinearity can be obtained by adding either the distributivity axiom or the contingency axiom to the basic Godel modal logic. Our approach can be extended to the intuitionistic modal logics in a similar manner. Our results can be viewed as an response to the open question posed by Alcocer and Gil, concerning the relationship between the finite model property and the normality of the logics in question. Our research shows that the issue of the normality property depends on the type of structures being considered, rather than the size of the structures themselves. Our results can be seen as an achievement in the quest for a deeper understanding of the connection between the algebraic and relational semantics for the family of the Godel modal logics. Our research can also be viewed as an extension to the results obtained by the same authors in a previous paper, where the focus was on the normal intuitionistic modal logic. Our results can be applied to the extension of the basic Godel modal logic with the axiom of duality, a property that can be derived from the applicable type of finite structures. Our results can be viewed as an response to the open question posed by the same authors in a previous paper, concerning the question whether the extension of the basic Godel modal logic with the axiom of duality and the contingency axiom is congruent with the applicable type of finite structures. LiDAR technology equips vehicles with precise sensors to scan and map their surroundings in 3D. Although the data they collect appears complex and intricate, the majority of current approaches to analyzing this data rely on the use of feature extractors which, despite effectiveness, can be costly in large-scale settings. Alternatively, learning-based methods have been explored for tasks such as detection, classification, and mapping, with numerous successful applications; however, the field lacks a comprehensive overview of LiDAR-specific techniques. This paper delves into various machine intelligence methods for processing LiDAR data, covering detection, classification, segmentation, and mapping, in addition to addressing related challenges and potential future developments in the field. Furthermore, we introduce LiDAR-specific datasets and introduce a new, open-source framework called Lidar-MI, designed to streamline the development of new LiDAR-based models, facilitated by easy data preprocessing and diverse tools for benchmarking various performance metrics. lidar-mi/lidar_mi.github.io

This paper introduces a novel approach to calculating global averages in a uniform random field defined by a given symmetric function over a spherical surface. The proposed method is compared to the conventional two-step strategy, and it is shown that it yields significantly better performance. Specifically, our approach exceeds the existing technique in complexity by a factor that scales with the square of the surface's dimension. As a result, this new algorithm is substantially more efficient in dealing with higher-dimensional data. As a mathematical contribution, we derive a general formula that expresses the standard inner product of two functions as a sum of individual components, and this outcome is then applied to several well-known functions. Additionally, the scope of this study is expanded to encompass nonuniform random fields and statistical estimators, and it is demonstrated that these extensions retain the same level of computational efficiency. Our numerical simulations validate the theoretical findings and reveal how the proposed algorithm's performance is impacted by the choice of parameters in both uniform and nonuniform settings. Furthermore, we explore the applicability of this algorithm to feature extraction in source separation problems. Our results indicate that this approach achieves comparable or superior accuracy to the conventional method, and it does so while significantly reducing the computational time. Our code is openly accessible and can be readily adapted to accommodate other applications. Our findings also suggest that there may be further speed optimizations achievable through the use of more efficient recurrence formulas, and we anticipate that our proposed framework will be valuable in addressing other recurrence-related problems. Our paper is a journal-eligible extension of our previous workshop paper. Our experiment setup was inspired by the works of Sahasrabuddhe (2003) and Subrahmanya (2005). Our study was supported by the grant AOARD-1041031 from the Air Force Office of Scientific Research (AFOSR). Our code is available at https://github.com/statistics-center/wasserstein-approximation and has been previously reported in our conference paper entitled "One-step Recurrences for Computing Signal Features" presented at the IEEE Data Science Workshop 2017. Our calculations were performed using MATLAB with the memory limit increased to 12 GB. Our data was sampled at a rate of 1000 Hz. The problem of finding neutrinos in ultra-high-energy cosmic particles remains a persistent challenge despite significant efforts made so far. In order to make progress in this area, a more in-depth analysis of the underlying theory is necessary. We would like to propose a mathematical framework that is based on spatial correlations and is capable of identifying neutrino sources. This framework is particularly suited for detecting neutrinos associated with hadronic cosmic rays, and it does not require any input from genetic cosmic rays. We have applied this method to an existing dataset of neutrino events as reported by the IceCube Neutrino Observatory and found evidence of spatial correlations with four events, including the famous track-like event known as IC-37. Furthermore, our analysis reveals that these neutrinos are likely produced by active galactic nuclei that are powerful enough to radiate neutrinos at a rate of $10^{39}$ calories per second, which is a rate that is observable from Earth. In contrast to traditional methods that look for spatial correlations on a galaxy scale, our method is more sensitive to neutrinos produced closer to Earth, which significantly expands the scope of our research. In fact, we are now looking at a sample of neutrinos that are produced at a distance of approximately 10 billion light-years, which is substantially closer than the galaxy-scale analysis. In order to confirm our findings, we plan to conduct further research using a more comprehensive dataset as reported by the IceCube Neutrino Observatory. In addition to verifying our discovery of spatial correlations, we also aim to gather more information about the neutrino events that we have previously identified, which include information on the direction of the neutrino events from Earth, the energy of the neutrino events, and the flux of the neutrino events as they approach Earth. The flow of liquid foams is significantly influenced by the interplay of two opposing forces: the tendency of the liquid to minimize its surface energy by reducing its extent, and the need to maintain continuity as it flows. This study reveals a previously unrecognized aspect of this balance, where the alignment of a surface pattern exerts an additional force that resists the motion of the foam. This force is shown to be a type of friction that varies depending on the angle between the foam and the patterned surface. It was also discovered that this frictional force can be exploited to create a "stick-slip" effect, where the foam experiences periods of slowed and rapid movement. Additionally, different components of this friction force were found to dominate in different scenarios, and were observed to shift from one state to another as the angle between the foam and the surface changes. The principles underlying these phenomena are thought to be applicable to other non-Newtonian fluids that exhibit similar behavior. The findings of this study have implications for the optimal design of surfaces for interacting with these types of fluids, and the potential for the development of novel technologies such as grippers and pumps that could take advantage of the unique properties of these fluids. This report details our methods and findings from participating in the 2017 ISIC challenge, where we placed third overall. The goal of this task was to classify dermatologic images containing carcinomas as either malignant or benign. To achieve this, we employed a multi-classifier approach combining both traditional spatial gray level co-occurrence matrix features and modern convolutional neural network architecture. Specifically, we utilized gray level co-occurrence matrix with entropy to identify outlier samples and integrated information from multiple orientations to enhance the discriminatory power of these features. We also explored the effectiveness of incorporating spatial information from the images' surroundings to aid in classification. Based on the results, our approach outperformed existing challenge winners, ending in third place with a carcinomatous accuracy rate of 77.31%. Further analysis revealed our method's reliability and strength lie in its robust identification of malignant carcinomas, achieving a precision rate of 81.89%. However, there is still room for improvement in differentiating between benign carcinomas and normal skin, with an accuracy rate of only 57.33%. To support further research, we have made our dataset replication guidelines publicly available. Building upon previous work, our solution improved upon existing challenges by introducing the use of entropy in feature selection and proposed alternative methods for CNNS comprising multiple experts. On top of this, we explored the challenge's data characteristics, analyzed the effects of overfitting, and included detailed replication guidelines. Finally, based on our findings, we have outlined potential future research directions for the ISIC challenge. The code and guidelines for reproducing our results are available at https://github.com/leobigodeep/ISIC2017. The document is available at https://drive.google.com/file/view/?id=1xXy1y1xX3Y6xX2xX4xX5X6xX7xX8xX9. The report's final version can be found at https://www.overleaf.com/project/blinds1dy4sf. The underlying data used for this study is derived from the ISIC 2017 challenge, which is in turn based on images gathered from the PH2 dataset, derived from dermoscopies collected by 10 different clinicians from various skin care centers located in Brazil, Germany, Italy, Poland, Spain, and the United Kingdom. These dermoscopies were conducted to examine patients with skin carcinomas characterized as melanomas, basal cell carcinomas, and squamous cell carcinomas, as well as a control group comprising normal skin

The steady-state fingering pattern that develops around a slowly moving bubble in a rectangular box filled with a different liquid, when the bubble is tilted, has been the subject of various studies. Research is extended to the case where the bubble is curved and moves slowly in a rectangular box filled with a different liquid, both with and without being tilted. The spread of the faster liquid forms a curved front around the bubble, which is stable and branched when the bubble is tilted and curved, respectively. The branched structure shares similarities with the Hansen-Yorke structure found in Rayleigh-Benard convection, and both are influenced by a dimensionless box aspect ratio. The boundary between these two states in the Rayleigh-Benard and Hele-Shaw systems both follow an "egg-chicken" problem, where the behavior depends on the relationship between two factors that determine them, and both become less stable as the box aspect ratio increases from its most compact to its most expansive extreme. The curvatures of the branched structure and the bubble are directly related, and both are influenced by the same "egg-chicken" problem, resulting in the coexistence of two "islands" of either stable or branched states when the bubble's curvature is negative or positive, respectively. The boundary between these "islands" breaks into two "seas" when the bubble's curvature is zero, and both "islands" shrink and eventually disappear when the box is either too compact or too expansive. The behavior of the Hele-Shaw system can be understood through a simple model that represents the spread of the faster liquid as the movement of a surface in the direction of the faster liquid, and both this model and research on the case where the bubble is tilted provide insight into the "egg-chicken" problem. The boundaries between stable and branched states in both the Hele-Shaw and Rayleigh-Benard systems are influenced by the same factors, and research on one can offer a deeper understanding of the other. The "egg-chicken" problem, where the behavior of the faster liquid in the Hele-Shaw cell depends on the relationship between two factors that determine the behavior of the boundary between stable and branched states, provides a general framework that can be applied to other problems, such as the movement of a bubble in the center of a curved Hele-Shaw cell, and both this problem and research on the case where the bubble is tilted are influenced by the same factors that determine the behavior of the boundary between stable and branched

Building on a novel idea, a new theoretical approach in mesoscopic research is presented, focusing on the expansion of a harmonic oscillator. Initially, the theory addresses the fundamental challenge of coherent states: the excessive increase in phase space volume. Additionally, an novel method is introduced for calculating physical observables in coherent states, leveraging the concept of Hamiltonian paths. Utilizing this framework, the expansion of an harmonic oscillator in one dimension is examined, with the result that the proposed theory successfully circumvents the critical issue of volume expansion in phase space. The results obtained from the new theory are compared with those from a commonly accepted approximation method, known as the Garside method, and the new theory is found to be more accurate. The scope of the study is then expanded to include the expansion of an harmonic oscillator in two dimensions, with the result that the proposed theory effectively addresses the prevalent problem of volume expansion in phase space, a issue encountered in the majority of calculations involving coherent states. The detection of ethynyl derivatives of cyclopentadiene, cycloheptatriene, and indene in TMC-1 is reported for the first time. Ethynyl derivatives of these structures have been theoretically modeled for comparison with observed interstellar spectral lines. From this analysis, the abundance of ethynyl derivatives relative to their parent molecules can be determined, with results indicating lower abundances for the ethynyl forms, specifically 0.75±0.12 for CCH and 0.47±0.09 for CN compared to their parent species. A possible explanation for these ratios is provided, suggesting the ethynyl forms have lower gas phase abundances due to their higher dipole moment. This hypothesis is supported by a comparison with CH3CCH, where the ratio of ethynyl to methyl forms is significantly higher, with a possible underlying reason being the larger electronegativity difference in this particular molecule. A relative abundance of the cyclopentadiene variant with the carbon chain oriented in a beta configuration to the cis form has also been observed, with a ratio of 0.58±0.19, offering further insight into the molecular structure and its underlying physics. Modeling of the spectral lines suggests a slightly larger internal temperature of 6.7 K for the cyclopentadiene component than the surrounding environment, with an estimated abundance of 0.085±0.015 when compared to H2. This discovery provides a key addition to the diverse range of organic molecules identified in TMC-1, a dense molecular cloud, and highlights the capability of radio astronomy to analyze the intricate chemistry within these interstellar formations. Furthermore, the observed ratios and structures of these ethynyl derivatives offer a chance to explore the complex chemical processes occurring in molecular clouds through the use of astrochemistry models, such as OMC2, which can predict the formation of diverse ethynyl derivatives of ring molecules like cyclopentadiene. Additionally, the detection of the cyclopentadiene variants at 18 GHz, a frequency previously inaccessible from sea level, has been made possible with the use of a telescope system operating at an elevation of 5060 meters in Chile. This breakthrough demonstrates the significance of investing in radio telescopes that can operate at higher frequencies, a decision that has paid off in this case by providing a groundbreaking scientific discovery. A combined dark fluid model has been developed which leverages a mixture of dark energy and dark matter to drive the cosmic acceleration, whereas the model's total density remains constant throughout the universe's evolution. This model succeeds in fitting the data from the Hubble diagram, supernovae, cosmic microwave background, Hubble flow, and structure formation constraints, outperforming a cosmological constant model while requiring fewer parameters. Additionally, the model's predictions for the universe's future behavior align with the Ricci scalar's current bounds and the stability constraints of the Hubble constant, despite the universe's density eventually dropping below the critical threshold in an eternally expanding state. This model exhibits physical coherence and simplicity, unlike other combined dark fluid models which often result in unphysically large estimates of the model's parameters. Furthermore, the model facilitates the derivation of an equation governing the universe's evolution similar to those derived from standard cosmological models, while also generating oscillatory behavior in the universe's expansion rate in an attempt to avoid the planar boundary crossing in the phase diagram. Nevertheless, the model fails in sufficiently addressing the cosmic acceleration issue when compared to its competitors within the same class of combined dark fluid models. Ultimately, the model falls short of the constraints derived from the data set used for its development. Another variation of this model, where the dark energy and dark matter components are separated in their respective pressures, also fit the observational constraints but resulted in an unstable system. Lastly, a discussion on the phase space's dimensionality, either two or four, is also presented in this study's expansion on combined dark fluid models.

Gaussian models representing functions based on Mat\'ern kernels have been widely used in various settings, including spatial and temporal applications.  While Mat\'ern kernels provide a comprehensive framework, their limitations arise when trying to model non-stationarity.  Recent developments in graph theory and statistical modeling have sparked interest in expanding Mat\'ern Gaussian processes to complex graph domains.  This work contributes novel constructions of non-stationary Mat\'ern Gaussian processes for exploring relationships within complex datasets, particularly-suited for exploratory data analysis.  Our non-stationary extensions of Mat\'ern Gaussian processes are shown to be statistically consistent when estimating parameters, and our new kernels also facilitate efficient and effective prediction.  To illustrate the practical advantages of these constructions, our research includes an analysis of synthetic data and a real-world application involving network analysis.  Our findings demonstrate that our non-stationary Mat\'ern Gaussian processes exhibit better performance compared to traditional approaches, leading to potential applications across multiple domains.  Our work on non-stationary Mat\'ern Gaussian processes is now publicly available through the RodyKit Python library Ryoko, making it easily accessible for further development and extension by the research community.  In addition, we outline several potential research extensions and pathways for future exploration within this exciting research area.  Our work is a product of the Kyoto University Statistics Initiative, a multidisciplinary research program dedicated to developing statistical theories, methods, and models, and we gratefully acknowledge the support received from this initiative.  We also wish to express our appreciation to Paul Brown for his helpful feedback and suggestions on this research.  Our research on non-stitionary Mat\'ern Gaussian processes has been successfully presented at the 2020 JSM Conference, and we are currently developing a follow-up study.  We would like to extend our special thanks to Xiangjing Yu for his assistance in testing our new Python constructor of graph Mat\'ern Gaussian processes.  Finally, we would like to acknowledge and show appreciation for the support provided by the Kyodo Press. We have developed a dynamic k-means algorithm that gradually adds objects one at a time to either existing clusters or a new one, choosing the one that reduces variance the most. This algorithm achieves a data-dependent guarantee, specifically a pre-set variance multiplier, for each new object added, ensuring that the variance of the optimal static solution is no more than a factor of (1+C) times the variance of the dynamic solution, where C is the number of clusters plus one. The concept of potential games was introduced by Monard and Merigi in 2009 and has since become a widely used framework for analyzing the equilibriums of multi-agent systems. Over the years, numerous extensions to this concept have been developed to address various complexities, including temporal cooperation, sequential decisions, and probabilistic interactions. However, despite its numerous contributions, the field lacks a comprehensive taxonomy to which existing research can be meaningfully categorized. To address this gap, we propose a hierarchical framework that organizes research related to potential games according to their focus on cooperative or competitive behaviors and the underlying structures of these games. Within this framework, existing research can be placed within one of four categories: (1) cooperative games that build upon existing structures, (2) cooperative games that introduce new structures, (3) noncooperative games that expand on existing structures, and (4) noncooperative games that introduce new structures. Furthermore, we position our own contributions, hierarchical games with probabilistic structures, within this framework, particularly highlighting our team's recent results published in reference [25] and [26]. By establishing a clear taxonomy, our hierarchical framework provides a valuable resource for researchers and practitioners to locate relevant research, as well as a sound foundation for further theoretical advancements in this field. Additionally, we include a comprehensive literature database that can serve as a starting point for in-depth analyses of various research topics. This database, which includes an overview of each referenced study, is made available at the following link: https://github.com/robmerrell/hpg-taxonomy. Through a case study involving hierarchical games, we demonstrate the value of our framework by using it to identify both the strengths and the weaknesses of existing research, as well as potential avenues for further contributions. Specifically, our team is currently exploring the concept of hierarchical games through a series of follow-up discussions and debates, as reflected in the accompanying appendix. This paper presents a generative model called Quasi-Periodic WaveNet (QPNet) to enhance the limited pitch control of WaveNet (WN) through pitch-sensitive dilated convolution neural networks (CNNs). WN achieves high-fidelity audio generation utilizing stacked dilated convolution layers as an autoregressive probabilistic model. However, the lack of global context hinders the model's ability to produce high-pitched sounds, likely due to the insufficient capture of quasi-periodic patterns in deep layer structures. To address this shortcoming, we introduce a pitch-sensitive dilated CNN (PD-CNN) layer that modulates the layer's periodical activity based on the input waveform's period, enabling the efficient capture of quasi-periodic patterns across multiple frequency bands. The PD-CNN's parameters are also waveform-dependent, allowing it to adapt to varying audio spectra. Despite operating as an autoregressive model, our results indicate that QPNet yields comparable performance to non-causal state-of-the-art WN and CNN-based generative models, while exhibiting the benefits of causicity, including pitch control through sampling rate. Furthermore, QPNet's pitch-sensitivity is achieved without the need for additional pitch-coded inputs, making it an efficient and practical model for raw waveform generation. Our findings are verified through multiple pitch-related objective evaluation metrics and a simple pitch-based melody reconstruction test. As such, this paper provides a viable solution to the limited pitch control of WaveNet and other autoregressive raw waveform generation models. Our model's code and demo audio files are available at https://github.com/ShangFengUCSD/Quasi-Periodic-WaveNet and will be shared at ICASSP 2021 Demo Session. Building upon this work, our team has recently developed a more advanced generative model called Raw Waveform Generation Network (RWGN) that outperforms all existing non-causal state-of-the-art models according to various objective evaluation metrics. This new model has also been open-sourced at https://github.com/ShangFengUCSD/Raw-Waveform-Generation-Network. Roadways require continuous maintenance to ensure public safety and efficiency, but traditional methods are costly and labor-intensive. This research demonstrates the development of a key technology within RoadAtlas, specifically the deep learning-based image analysis algorithm, which can automatically extract features from images, classify them as healthy or damaged, and even characterize the type of damage present. This algorithm's effectiveness was validated using over 5000 labeled images covering eight high-priority highway defect types. Furthermore, a feature extraction technique known as invariant cropping was discovered and found to significantly improve the model's scalability and overall performance. This research advances the development of RoadAtlas, a revolutionary platform that has the potential to transform the way highway maintenance is conducted through rapid, cost-effective detection of defects and characterization thereof. This technology is critical for the development of smart transportation systems and the integration of artificial intelligence into infrastructure management. This is because it demonstrates the possibility of using deep learning-based computer vision in an real-world, high-stakes application where misclassification can have serious consequences. This is further underscored by the fact that there is currently a scarcity of research being conducted along highways, particularly in areas with dense vegetation, which presents an significant barrier to the development of real-world, high-performance computer vision applications. This research addresses this gap by developing a high-performance, real-world computer vision application from scratch. This achievement is all the more impressive considering the difficulties encountered, such as building a large, high-quality dataset, overcoming the limitations of current deep learning architectures, and mitigating the effects of dynamic environmental factors, which are all key challenges that typically hinder the development of real-world computer vision applications. This research provides several valuable contributions to the field of computer vision, specifically in the area of highway defect detection.
